title:
Not All Bots are Equal: 
Chatbot Roles and Human Interaction in Online Chat Groups
affiliations: University of Miami Herbert Business School, Miami Herbert Business School, University of Miami and University of Miami Herbert Business School

detail.title:
Not All Bots are Equal: 
Chatbot Roles and Human Interaction in Online Chat Groups
detail.abstract: Chatbots are ubiquitous in online chat groups, but their effects on group interaction remain understudied. Prior chatbot research has largely emphasized cue-based heterogeneity in dyadic human-chatbot exchanges, while recent work in multiparty settings has examined chatbot effects without considering how role heterogeneity shapes outcomes. Integrating the functional role theory with computers as social actors (CASA) framework, we conceptualize chatbots roles along three dimensions: role positioning, role enactment, and role competency. Role positioning captures the functional position a chatbot occupies in the group, distinguishing algorithmic governance chatbots that regulate group activity from algorithmic affordance chatbots that support member activities. Role enactment captures how human members direct requests to the chatbot, distinguishing command-based from command-free designs. Role competency captures the chatbot's interpretive capacity, distinguishing rule-based from AI-enabled designs. Analyzing data from Telegram chat groups, we classify chatbots using text embeddings and hierarchical clustering, then estimate their effects on group participation and emotional expression using a matrix completion estimator with covariate-balancing weights. Our results show, first, that chatbot role positioning produces divergent effects, with governance chatbots removing disruptive content and increasing participation with null effect on emotional expression, whereas affordance chatbots substitute for human replies and suppress both. Second, chatbot role enactment moderates these effects. For governance chatbots, command-based designs allow administrators to configure enforcement to group-specific norms and increase participation, whereas command-free designs apply fixed rules that may diverge from those norms and suppress emotional expression. For affordance chatbots, command-free designs amplify the substitution of chatbot replies for human ones and suppress participation, whereas command-based designs structure human-chatbot exchange around task-oriented requests and suppress emotional expression. Third, chatbot role competency moderates and reverse role-positioning effects. AI-enabled governance chatbots produce a substantially larger positive participation increase than rule-based ones; AI-enabled affordance chatbots reverse the negative participation effect of rule-based ones and neutralize the suppression of emotional expression. Our study extends the CASA framework from a cuebased to a role-based account of chatbot effects. Additionally, we provide empirical evidence on the effect of chatbot roles on group interaction by showing that the different chatbot roles constitute significant sources of variation in online chat groups.

title: The Economic Forcing Function: Compute Constraints, Hybrid Swarm Architectures, and the Inversion of the Infrastructure Stranding Thesis

detail.title: The Economic Forcing Function: Compute Constraints, Hybrid Swarm Architectures, and the Inversion of the Infrastructure Stranding Thesis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study because it does not involve human participants, patient data, animal subjects, or primary data collection. The work is based on publicly available literature, financial reports, industry data, and secondary sources.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: The deceleration of Moore's Law and Dennard scaling has imposed an escalating cost ceiling on centralised computation. Frontier model training compute is growing exponentially at 5x per year since 2020 (doubling every 5.2 months) while the financial cost of training is increasing at 3.5x per year (doubling every 7 months), far outstripping the ~1.37x annual improvement in hardware price-performance. This paper presents empirical and architectural evidence that this compute ceiling acts as a key rate constraint on labour displacement (G_D), driving a transition to a distributed, three-layer Hybrid Swarm Architecture. We show that this transition suggests a potential inversion of the dominant infrastructure stranding thesis: the massive $700B-$725B aggregate hyperscaler capital buildout projected for 2026 may be better interpreted not as a stranded asset bubble, but rather as the productive centralised hub of a coexisting human-AI economy (AGI-C). We present verified May 2026 data on hyperscaler capex, Nvidia Blackwell standard deployments ($81.6B record Q1 FY2027 revenue), illustrative indicators of enterprise workload repatriation (including a Cloudian-commissioned survey of 203 IT decision-makers showing a 93 per cent repatriation rate), and near-future 1.58-bit ternary on-device co-design. This formalises the Economic Forcing Function (EFF) as the physical and economic rate-limiter of labour market transition speeds, suggesting how the depreciation and capital pressures identified by bubble theorists act as structural mechanisms driving a metamorphic evolution that preserves and sustains infrastructure value.

detail.abstract: This article develops Agentic Capital as a measurable and econometrically testable productive category of the agentic economy. The core argument is that models, data, robots, compute, protocols and human-sovereignty systems are no longer auxiliary digital inputs; they increasingly constitute a composite stock of productive assets that enables economic action to be selected, executed, verified and governed. To operationalise this concept, the study constructs a six-pillar Agentic Capital framework composed of model capital, data capital, robotic physical capital, compute capital, protocol capital and human sovereignty capital. The methodology adapts the diagnostics-first logic of the Gondauri Index by using robust normalisation, additive and geometric aggregation, balance and gap diagnostics, non-compensatory adjustment and scenario pathways. The key transformation is the Gondauri-adjusted Agentic Capital Index, which integrates macro-financial resilience into the agentic-capital measurement architecture so that technological readiness is not interpreted separately from systemic resilience. Empirically, the article applies a country-year panel design for nine economies over 2005-2024 and estimates the relationship between agentic capital and labour productivity growth through a layered econometric strategy. The analysis combines pooled OLS, random effects, fixed effects, Hausman model selection, panel unit-root diagnostics, Pesaran cross-sectional dependence testing, Driscoll-Kraay robust standard errors, dynamic panel GMM, IV-2SLS, panel quantile regression, Hansen-style threshold estimation, mediation analysis, component-level fixed effects and robustness checks. The results indicate that geometric agentic capital is positively associated with labour productivity performance, that structural imbalance weakens the maturity of the system, and that human sovereignty and governance conditions shape the productivity value of agentic systems. The article contributes to capital theory by shifting the analytical focus from accumulated productive assets toward accumulated capacity for governed economic action. It also provides a reproducible empirical architecture for assessing how countries, sectors and firms can transform AI readiness into legitimate, auditable and productivity-relevant agentic capacity.

title: Digital Identity, Government-to-Person (G2P) Payment Delivery and Uptake of Social Assistance
affiliations: Cornell University - Samuel Curtis Johnson Graduate School of Management, Indian Institute of Management Bangalore, Indian School of Business - Operations Management and Indian School of Business

detail.title: Digital Identity, Government-to-Person (G2P) Payment Delivery and Uptake of Social Assistance
detail.abstract: Governments are increasingly using digital unique identification numbers (UIDs), often linked to citizens' biometrics, to deliver social welfare payments. On the one hand, UID-linked payments reduce frictions in cash access through an additional channel of Banking Agents (BAs), typically nano-store owners with biometric-enabled micro-ATMs. On the other hand, implementation complexity and low financial awareness of citizens can increase frictions in cash access through incorrect linkages in the account mapper and redirection of payments to accounts that citizens are unaware of. Methodology: We examine the impact of UID-linked systems in the context of India's workfare program under which citizens in rural areas have a legal right to demand up to 100 days of work. We hypothesize that the increased (reduced) friction in cash access for citizens will reduce (increase) their confidence in the workfare program and, consequently, their future uptake of work. We test our hypothesis using 22.84 million payments to 1.91 million citizens, of which 57% transition to UID-linked payments. Using a unique cohort-wise difference-indifferences design, we find that average quarterly earnings per citizen rise by INR 281.07, a 41.84% increase after transition. Citizens with a proximate BA (within three kilometers of their village) see a 44.03% quarterly wage increase, vis-à-vis 37.76% for those without. Among transitioned citizens, 26% experience wage redirection. For them, the impact of UID-linked system is insignificant, compared to a 49.98% increase for those whose accounts were mapped correctly. BA presence slightly mitigates this: redirected citizens with a proximate BA see a 4.85% increase, while the impact remains insignificant for those without a proximate BA. Implications: As governments increasingly adopt UID-linked systems, we present the first long-term evidence that the impact of these systems is shaped by the broader institutional ecosystem of public programs, financial institutions, and BAs, within which they are implemented.

title: Harnessing Agent Skills: Architectural Patterns and a Reference Architecture for Skill-Mediated LLM Agents
affiliations: , CSIRO, CSIRO, CSIRO,  and CSIRO

detail.title: Harnessing Agent Skills: Architectural Patterns and a Reference Architecture for Skill-Mediated LLM Agents
detail.abstract: Agent skills externalise reusable agent-facing behavioural knowledge and guidance as persistent artefacts that can be discovered, activated, and interpreted by LLM agents. Although a skill artefact is static at rest, its architectural responsibilities arise in use, when the artefact is selected for a run, bound to context and authority constraints, interpreted by a stochastic agent, and recorded as run evidence. We call this run-specific relation skill-in-use. This paper studies agent skill harnessing: the architectural responsibilities that govern the transition from skill artefacts to skill-in-use, bound the executable consequences associated with skill-in-use, and capture evidence for attribution, verification, repair, and evolution. Through a multivocal literature review of 37 systems and 51 papers, we derive a catalogue of ten architectural patterns (five core, five supporting) for skill harnessing and synthesise them into a reference architecture with four responsibility layers: Supply Chain, Mediation, Execution Control, and Evidence & Feedback. We evaluate the architecture through cross-instantiation across 8 selected systems. The resulting patterns and reference architecture provide a vocabulary and diagnostic frame for analysing skill-harnessing responsibilities across agent systems.

title: Internal AI Ethics Committees: Window Dressing or Working Mechanism? A Comparative Study of Corporate Governance Structures

detail.title: Internal AI Ethics Committees: Window Dressing or Working Mechanism? A Comparative Study of Corporate Governance Structures
detail.abstract: Since 2018, enterprises across technology, financial services, healthcare, and retail have established internal AI ethics committees, advisory boards, and responsible AI teams in response to public pressure, regulatory signals, and investor scrutiny. But do these structures produce measurable governance outcomes, or do they function primarily as reputational insurance-organizational mechanisms whose primary output is the appearance of ethical oversight rather than its substance? This paper conducts a comparative analysis of internal AI ethics governance structures across a sample of 30 enterprises, evaluating them on four dimensions: mandate clarity (decision-making authority versus advisory role), organizational independence (reporting lines and insulation from product revenue pressure), outcome measurement (demonstrable cases where the committee changed product design or halted deployments), and stakeholder legitimacy (representation of affected communities in governance deliberations). The paper introduces the AI Ethics Committee Effectiveness Model (AECEM), a diagnostic framework that identifies three governance archetypes-Performative (window dressing), Procedural (process-compliant but outcome-weak), and Substantive (producing measurable governance impact)-and maps the structural conditions that determine which archetype an organization's AI ethics governance occupies. Drawing structural parallels with the evolution of corporate sustainability committees-another governance mechanism that began as reputational insurance but, under regulatory and investor pressure, evolved into a substantive function in some organizations-the paper identifies the conditions under which internal AI ethics committees transition from performative to effective. The paper concludes with implications for Chief Ethics Officers designing governance structures, corporate governance researchers studying institutional evolution, responsible AI practitioners operating within these committees, and ESG analysts evaluating AI governance quality.

title: From Observer To Governor: Reconstructing Evidentiary Accountability In Autonomous Multi-Agent Accounting And Aml/Ctf Systems

detail.title: From Observer To Governor: Reconstructing Evidentiary Accountability In Autonomous Multi-Agent Accounting And Aml/Ctf Systems

detail.abstract: Rapid integration of the autonomous multi-agent systems of artificial intelligence to accounting, anti-money laundering, auditing and Counter-Terrorism Financing (AML/CTF) environment is generating a fundamental transformation in the accountability of institutions. While the existing model of governance continues in relying heavily on the retrospective supervision and oversight of humans in the loop, these approaches are increasingly not capable of governing the autonomous system of finance, which is recursive in governance and under which decision-making authority is computationally fragmented throughout the interacting agents of AI. Building directly on the scepticism gap that is established in the paper one, the current study argues that the core challenge that faces the accounting profession is no longer considered to be epistemic opacity, but Accountability Fragmentation leading to the collapse of the evidentiary governance. Traditional models of audit are designed for the environments in which the human actors are reasonably capable of reconstructing the transactional intent, accountability pathway and professional judgment. The autonomous system of multi-agent destabilises the assumptions by distribution of the operational logic throughout the algorithmic interactions, which might not be adequately capable of developing a new architecture of governance centred on the AHAA framework, recursive loop of Accountability, adaptive Accountability system and governance receipts. The paper is proposing the shift from the reactive monitoring of compliance towards embedded governance of evidentiary in which accountability becomes computationally infrastructural rather than being procedurally symbolic in nature. Through the help of conceptual simulations as well as stress testing methodologies of governance, the paper demonstrates how forensic auditability, suspicious integrity of matter reporting, and institutional accountability might be reconstructed in the autonomous systems of finance. The study is contributing to the emerging field of agentic accounting governance by establishing the conceptual foundation regarding future research on autonomous auditability, recursive architecture of compliance and Computational duty of fiduciary.

title: Interpretation of Statutes - Different Prospective in Indian Legal System
affiliations: Business School, The School of Science Management and Commerce

detail.title: Interpretation of Statutes - Different Prospective in Indian Legal System
detail.abstract: Interpretation of statutes is one of the most essential functions of the judiciary within the Indian legal system. Statutes enacted by Parliament and State Legislatures often contain ambiguities, inconsistencies, and evolving meanings that require judicial clarification. The Indian judiciary has developed multiple interpretative approaches such as literal interpretation, golden rule, mischief rule, purposive interpretation, harmonious construction, and constitutional interpretation to ensure justice and legislative intent. This research paper examines the concept, nature, and importance of statutory interpretation in India and analyses different judicial perspectives adopted by Indian courts. The paper further discusses constitutional dimensions, judicial activism, and modern trends in interpretation in the context of social justice and changing legal realities. The research highlights how interpretation of statutes acts as a bridge between legislation and justice delivery in contemporary India.

title: HUMANE Research: A Practical Methodology Guide for Applying an Ethical AI Framework in Social Science Research
affiliations: Universidad Panamericana

detail.title: HUMANE Research: A Practical Methodology Guide for Applying an Ethical AI Framework in Social Science Research
detail.abstract: The integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into academic research has outpaced the development of practical methodological guidance. While ethical frameworks for AI use in research exist at a normative level, researchers in the social sciences lack concrete, step-by-step tools for implementing them in daily practice. This paper presents a practical methodology guide based on the HUMANE framework — an acronym for six operational principles: Honest disclosure, Understand your work, Master your sources, Advance knowledge, Navigate your research, and Expose and defend. For each principle, this guide provides actionable decision rules, self-audit checklists, and illustrative examples drawn from real research contexts. The guide is designed to be immediately applicable by individual researchers working independently, without requiring institutional infrastructure or specialized training. A literature search of Scopus (TITLE-ABS-KEY: “HUMANE” OR “research workflow” OR “academic integrity” AND “artificial intelligence” OR “generative AI” AND “methodology” OR “practical guide”; 2022–2026, Articles and Reviews) yielded 226 qualifying records, confirming an active and growing literature on AI, research integrity, and practical guidance, but revealing limited frameworks that address the full research workflow from question formulation through public defense.

title: The Borrowed Tongue AI Frame Colonization and the Cognitive Closure of the Accountability Loop

detail.title: The Borrowed Tongue AI Frame Colonization and the Cognitive Closure of the Accountability Loop

declarations.declarationOfInterest: no
declarations.ethicsApproval: not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: self

detail.abstract: The first paper in this sequence established that confident fabrication is endemic across the generative AI supply chain regardless of model tier and falls hardest where verification cost is highest. The second showed the structural mechanism: a seven-node chain built so that no party is responsible for what the affected party receives, a chain that closes into a loop in which the missing developer is a role never assigned. This paper asks the cognitive question those findings make necessary: through what mechanism does a frame imported from the model's training corpus become the user's own thought, adopted as native rather than recognized as borrowed? The paper advances a single thesis, that under specifiable conditions AI output does not influence cognition alongside native faculty but occupies the structural position of cognitive faculty, performing its function while remaining undetectable as foreign from inside. Two biological metaphors serve as analytical engines rather than illustration: the cuckoo names the installation mechanism through trickery and tuning calibrated to host vulnerability; the tongue louse names functional replacement in which operational adequacy and structural exploitation co-occur indistinguishably from inside. A third metaphor, the cordyceps, names the directed-behavior dimension by which the colonized host produces outputs that feed the corpus that trains the next generation of borrowed tongues. The paper records two registers of primary observation, cultural and intimate, in which the supply-chain loop closes through cognition rather than through the chain alone. It identifies the verifier as the load-bearing accountability node whom the surrounding social system penalizes for performing the function. The paper's own production is part of its evidence.

title: When Everyone Gets the Same Spark: How AI Inspiration Shapes Creative Diversity in the Creator Economy
affiliations: , University of Mannheim - Business School and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Management Science (MS)

detail.title: When Everyone Gets the Same Spark: How AI Inspiration Shapes Creative Diversity in the Creator Economy

publicationDetails.journalName: MIT Sloan School of Management Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: AI models are increasingly embedded in creative platforms as upstream sources of inspiration. We study how such AI-assisted inspiration affects the amount and creative diversity of realized output when many producers draw on a shared generative system. Our setting is YouTube’s rollout of the Inspiration Tab, an ideation feature that suggests video ideas, hooks, and storylines but does not generate videos. Exploiting regional variation in access between U.S. and European creators, we estimate difference-in-differences models on a matched panel of incumbent YouTube creators. First, access increases video production by 4.1%. Heterogeneity analyses reveal that the increase is consistent with the treatment relaxing an upstream ideation constraint conditional on complementary implementation capabilities, rather than simply lowering the marginal cost of producing additional videos. Second, access also changes the composition of creativity. Second, treated creators' videos become more similar to their own prior output along semantic and topical dimensions, reducing within-creator diversity, while similarity across creators is unchanged. Therefore AI-assisted inspiration intensifies localized exploitation around creator-specific niches rather than inducing ecosystem-wide convergence. Downstream, treated creators receive 12.47% more total views, but views per video fall, suggesting that additional supply expands aggregate attention while lowering average returns to AI-enabled output. We find no evidence of significant entry by new creators. These results show that even when AI is not deployed in production, it can substantially alter the amount and creative diversity of realized output. In creative markets, therefore, ideation-stage AI affects realized output by relaxing an important upstream constraint, but realized output remains constrained by the complementary capabilities and experience needed to implement suggested ideas, as well as shaped by creators’ incentives for exploitation and audience legitimacy.

title: BEYOND THE SPREADSHEET: AI Tools and the Future of Small Tax Practice

detail.title: BEYOND THE SPREADSHEET: AI Tools and the Future of Small Tax Practice
detail.abstract: Small tax and CPA firms represent the majority of accounting practice in the United States, yet they have largely been left out of the conversation surrounding artificial intelligence adoption. This paper examines how AI tools, with a focus on Anthropic's Claude and Claude Cowork, can be applied to real compliance workflows including bank statement categorization, workpaper preparation, and client document review. Using a full year of AI-generated bank statements for a fictitious small business, this paper documents and compares three workflows: manual categorization in Excel, categorization via Claude's standard chat interface, and categorization via Claude Cowork. The results demonstrate a reduction in processing time from 2 hours and 15 minutes to 1 minute and 17 seconds, with Cowork producing a structurally superior output. The paper also addresses data privacy obligations, AICPA professional standards, and Treasury Circular 230 considerations that practitioners must understand before adoption. The conclusion is that AI tools represent a meaningful productivity opportunity for small firms today, with important constraints on client data handling that are current rather than permanent.

title: Architectural Data Isolation in Deterministic Personalisation Systems

detail.title: Architectural Data Isolation in Deterministic Personalisation Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder and CEO of Smart Astro Ltd, the company that developed and operates the reference implementation discussed in this paper. No external funding was received for conducting this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper presents a privacy and data-isolation architecture case study and does not report experiments involving human participants, patients, animals, or customer-specific personal data. No ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for conducting this study. The research and development work was independently conducted by the author.

detail.abstract: The dominant assumption in AI personalisation is that effective personalised output requires persistent identity. This paper challenges that assumption for Deterministic Guidance Systems (DGS)-systems in which identical structured inputs always produce identical computational outputs, independent of runtime state or session history. For such systems, personalisation variables and sensitive identity variables are orthogonal: computation is fully specified by constitutional inputs without behavioural accumulation or cross-session identity linkage. This paper presents the minimal-PII architectural pattern for DGS, comprising three mechanisms: (1) a structured input model in which constitutional variables fully specify personalised computation without behavioural profiling; (2) a channelnative identity abstraction layer that maps platform-assigned identifiers to channelscoped references without maintaining a cross-channel identity graph; and (3) a deterministic computation engine whose outputs are cryptographically anchored without embedding personal data in the proof record. The resulting architecture supports structural alignment with GDPR, India's DPDP Act, and CCPA through a single design decision-data minimisation at the computation layer. A production implementation demonstrates this pattern across multiple structured decision domains and delivery channels. The paper establishes the architectural principles, threat model, and broader implications for privacy-preserving deterministic AI system design.

title: Human-First AI in Organizations: A Conceptual Framework for Ethical Implementation and Management Practice

detail.title: Human-First AI in Organizations: A Conceptual Framework for Ethical Implementation and Management Practice

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable — this is a conceptual article; no human-subject data were collected.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Purpose-The purpose of this paper is to define Human-First AI as an organisational philosophy in which the deployment question is not whether AI should replace human work but which tasks AI should absorb and how the freed human capacity should be redirected within the organisation. The framework distinguishes itself from adjacent system-design and compliance-focused frameworks of human-centred and responsible AI by taking an explicit position on the labourallocation consequences of deployment. Design/methodology/approach-The article applies integrative theory synthesis (Jaakkola, 2020) to combine AI ethics scholarship with established management theories of selfdetermination, organisational justice, meaningful work, job design, and the automationaugmentation paradox. A five-stage analytical process-thematic mapping, gap identification, construct clustering, pillar development, and indicator derivation-is used and documented in the appendices. Findings-Human-First AI is conceptualised through four pillars-Human Dignity Preservation, Augmentation Over Automation, Transparent Human-AI Collaboration, and Meaningful Work Protection-unified by critical thinking as a moderating mechanism. Seven testable propositions are derived; observable organisational indicators are specified; and a fourstage maturity model grounded in capability maturity theory (Paulk et al., 1993) and institutionalisation theory (Greenwood et al., 2002) is proposed. Originality/value-The framework's defining feature is a fourfold commitment which adjacent AI frameworks decline to make: (i) AI substitutes tasks, not people, with freed human capacity redirected to higher-meaning work within the role; (ii) workers participate in deciding which tools serve them, since tools deployed without worker buy-in are rarely used and are read as competitive threats rather than as instruments of their own work; (iii) the criterion for which work AI should absorb is the work workers themselves identify as draining and bureaucratic; and (iv) the strategic-economic case for redirection over substitution is at least as strong as the ethical one, since substitution-by-default generates vendor-concentration risk, loss of accumulated organisational context, and compressed delivery capacity (Brynjolfsson, 2022; Williamson, 1985; Smids et al., 2020). The article (a) clarifies Human-First AI as an organisational, rather than design or compliance, philosophy; (b) links AI ethics to management scholarship on dignity, justice, meaning, and stakeholder governance across previously disconnected literatures; and (c) provides an operationalisation that supports both empirical scale development and management pedagogy. A pilot application of the framework in a higher-education context is in design, with data collection planned for academic year 2026-2027 and results to be reported separately.

title: Customer Segmentation Analytics in Retail: An Empirical Study Using K-Means Clustering, UMAP, and BG/NBD Lifetime Value Modelling
affiliations: University of Liverpool

detail.title: Customer Segmentation Analytics in Retail: An Empirical Study Using K-Means Clustering, UMAP, and BG/NBD Lifetime Value Modelling
detail.abstract: Despite growing investment in customer data infrastructure across the retail sector, the translation of transaction records into differentiated, value-weighted marketing decisions remains underdeveloped in both practice and the academic literature. This paper develops and empirically validates an integrated analytical pipeline-combining RFM feature engineering, K-means customer segmentation, UMAP non-linear dimensionality reduction, and BG/NBD + Gamma-Gamma lifetime value modelling-applied to a publicly available retail dataset of 3,800 customers and 136,571 transactions. The pipeline produces well-validated segment structure (K = 4; silhouette coefficient = 0.4767; Calinski-Harabasz index = 1,987; ANOVA η² ranging from 0.7581 to 0.9176, all p < 0.001; 20-seed ARI stability = 0.997) and segment-level CLV predictions that are both statistically robust and commercially actionable: Loyal Premium customers (15.2% of the base) carry a mean predicted 12-month CLV of £441, compared to £3 for Dormant/At-Risk customers — a 140-to-1 disparity that directly informs differential marketing investment.

title: Criminal Capture and The Reallocation of Political Participation
affiliations: University of Milan - Faculty of Law

detail.title: Criminal Capture and The Reallocation of Political Participation

publicationDetails.journalName: BAFFI Centre on Economics, Finance & Regulation Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: How do citizens react to the criminal capture of state institutions? Do they simply reduce their engagement with public life or do they reallocate it across different channels of participation? With an event-study design, I show that revealing collusion between Italian public officials and organized criminal groups leads to a modest reduction in electoral turnout. However, collusion episodes are also followed by a sizable increase in the participation of citizens to the activities of civil society organizations fighting organized crime. I analyze the causal mechanisms behind this effect with an original survey experiment. Receiving information about the incidence of collusion increases citizens’ concerns about organized criminal groups while decreasing their confidence that the state will contrast them. This induces reallocation: collusion weakens electoral participation while strengthening civic engagement. These findings complement the existing literature about the effects of state capture on citizens’ behavior, showing that it can foster their engagement in non-traditional forms of political participation.

title: We Can't Agree to Disagree, Formally: Aumann's Theorem and Assumption Accounting in Lean
affiliations: , , ,  and

detail.title: We Can't Agree to Disagree, Formally: Aumann's Theorem and Assumption Accounting in Lean

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Chen, Eltschig, Ono, and Zhang are affiliated with Axiom Math, which provided computational and infrastructure resources in support of this project.
declarations.funderStatement: All authors received support from their affiliated institutions. This work was conducted while Kominers was visiting the Technological Innovation, Entrepreneurship, and Strategic Management (TIES) Group at the MIT Sloan School of Management; he greatly appreciates their hospitality.

detail.abstract: We present a Lean formalization of Aumann's agreement theorem as a case study in assumption accounting for economic theory. The formalization makes precise the chain of reasoning by which common knowledge of posterior probabilities, together with a common prior, yields agreement. The key step is an aggregation principle: posterior constancy on the information cells inside a common-knowledge event implies the same posterior value on the common-knowledge event itself. In finite models the required aggregation is automatic; in general measurable spaces it requires explicit measurability and countability hypotheses. In the Lean development, both arise from a single source: positivity of each information cell both makes the ratio defining the posterior well-defined and forces the information partition to be countable, which in turn justifies the countable additivity used in the aggregation step. The final theorem is stated modularly, replacing the common prior by equality of conditional probabilities on the common-knowledge cell, with the usual common-prior theorem recovered as a special case. The same partition and posterior infrastructure also supports a Lean formalization, produced with automated proving assistance, of the Monderer–Samet p-belief variant in which weakening common knowledge turns exact agreement into a quantitative approximate-agreement bound. Our work illustrates how formalization can not only verify a proof, but also delineate which assumptions support each step of the logic—thus enabling exact agreement about what agreement assumes.

title: A Study Of Rural-Urban Migration And Paradox Of Unemployment: Causes, Challenges, And Consequences
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: A Study Of Rural-Urban Migration And Paradox Of Unemployment: Causes, Challenges, And Consequences
detail.abstract: Rural-Urban migration has become a significant socioeconomic phenomenon in India, driven by the pursuit of better employment opportunities, higher income, improved education, healthcare, and living standards. A paradox emerges when migrants face limited opportunities in urban areas, resulting in urban unemployment. This study examines the ruralurban migration and the paradox of unemployment with particular attention to the factors influencing migration decisions, labour market outcomes, gender roles, and the effectiveness of government interventions. The research adopts a mixed approach based on secondary data from the Census of India reports, PLFS and NSSO publications, NITI AAYOG reports and other academic journals. The study is guided by the Harris-Todaro Model and Lewis Dual Sector Model to explain migration patterns and labour market dynamics. It also identifies patterns of circular migration, where individuals return to rural areas during economic hardships and then return to urban areas in search of work. Furthermore, gender roles significantly influence migration decisions and employment outcomes, while limited awareness and accessibility of welfare schemes reduce the effectiveness of government initiatives

title: Measuring the Impact of Impact Measurement
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business, University of California, Berkeley, Harvard University - Business School (HBS) and Harvard University - Business School (HBS)

detail.title: Measuring the Impact of Impact Measurement
detail.abstract: Impact measurement is central to impact investing and social entrepreneurship, yet little is known about whether firms benefit privately from measuring impact. We conduct the first randomized controlled trial of an impact measurement intervention among high-growth social enterprises in India. Treated firms exhibit nearly twice as much revenue growth and raise nearly twice as much capital as control firms. In a companion experiment with early-stage investors, we find that investors respond strongly to quantified impact metrics but not to generic qualitative impact statements. Together, our results show that impact measurement can shape firm growth and capital allocation.

The AI tools were used exclusively for editorial and structural optimization and did not contribute to the intellectual originality or the substantive claims of this research.

detail.abstract:
Black maternal mortality in the United States remains a persistent public health emergency, yet existing surveillance and governance models often fail to identify or address preventable deaths. This paper examines the "affluence paradox" in Collier County, Florida—a region characterized by extreme wealth alongside a significant agricultural labor population that faces documented obstetric disparities. Using race-stratified maternal mortality data from FL Health CHARTS (2005–2024), this study documents how current aggregate reporting mechanisms mask episodic mortality spikes in the Black maternal population, rendering the crisis statistically invisible and exempt from corrective governance.

Drawing on structural racism theory, institutional betrayal, and the framework of administrative violence, the paper diagnoses five interlocking layers of systemic failure that insulate healthcare institutions from accountability. To address these gaps, the author introduces the Trauma-Informed Maternal Health System (TIMHS) accreditation framework. This novel regulatory model translates SAMHSA’s six trauma-informed principles into enforceable governance standards for birthing facilities, explicitly linking compliance to Medicaid reimbursement and value-based purchasing. By providing a legislative bill template and a pilot strategy for Collier County, this research offers a replicable, high-specificity roadmap for structural policy reform. This paper concludes that Black maternal mortality is not a clinical inevitability but a structural governance failure that can only be dismantled through the force of law and equity-aligned fiscal incentives.

title: The Asymmetric Macro-Financial and Socio-Psychiatric Overhead of Geopolitical # Frictions: A Structural Analysis of the GCC Economies (2024-2026)

detail.title: The Asymmetric Macro-Financial and Socio-Psychiatric Overhead of Geopolitical # Frictions: A Structural Analysis of the GCC Economies (2024-2026)
detail.abstract:
This paper provides a comprehensive, empirical evaluation of the macroeconomic, logistical, and psychosocial transmission mechanisms altering the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) economies in the wake of the regional conflict matrix spanning from late 2024 into the first half of 2026. Operating under the constraints of unilateral U.S. dollar pegs, GCC states have faced an asymmetric economic shock characterized by volatile oil revenues, shifting fiscal breakeven thresholds, and cost-push imported inflation.

By modeling maritime logistical frictions, this study illustrates how international risk re-pricing—specifically the escalation of Joint War Committee (JWC) war risk insurance premiums—has driven an institutional pivot toward continental and multi-modal transit networks, cementing the geo-economic role of alternative land corridors, particularly through Turkey.

Crucially, this research expands standard macroeconomic paradigms by introducing a novel microeconomic indicator: the socioeconomic overhead of labor anxiety and the utilization rates of psychiatric and counseling services within major urban centers like Dubai and Riyadh.

The empirical findings demonstrate that while sovereign wealth funds (SWFs) successfully function as liquidity buffers to safeguard national currencies, the compounding environmental stress has diminished effective labor productivity and altered expatriate retention dynamics. This interdisciplinary framework offers vital strategic insights for policymakers navigating the intersection of conflict, maritime risk management, and human capital resilience in high-risk zones.

title: No Edge Without Information: An Empirical Study of Tradeability in Decentralized-Exchange-Only Cryptocurrencies
affiliations: UNIP - Universidade Paulista

detail.title: No Edge Without Information: An Empirical Study of Tradeability in Decentralized-Exchange-Only Cryptocurrencies
detail.abstract: This paper makes a single argument: in decentralized-exchange (DEX) markets of small, mostly non-CEX-listed tokens, a long-only, realistically-costed trader has no detectable edge that price information can supply; the only structure that survives a null is non-price and merely predicts which tokens crash; and the binding obstacle to finding more is survivorship, not method. On a survivorship-aware corpus of 4,990 DEX pairs across 27 blockchains reconstructed from on-chainderived OHLCV, we assemble the case in five movements, every claim benchmarked against a bar-shuffled null and reported over the full distribution of outcomes rather than cherry-picked winners. (i) Price-based timing shows no detectable edge at any horizon (intraday, swing, cross-sectional, cross-chain): real data performs no better than, and usually worse than, its own shuffle, on a process that is negativedrift, heavy-tailed (pooled Hill α ≈ 1.3-1.5, though the per-coin median is α ≈ 3), volatility-clustered, and negatively autocorrelated, which is adverse to longs and may in part be a stale-price microstructure effect. (ii) That negative is structural, not methodological: it survives the intrabar exit convention (≤23 bp/trade), stricter walk-forward selection, and cost mis-specification (the median strategy loses even at zero cost). (iii) The strategies practitioners actually use fail too, net of cost (market-neutral hedging, launch timing, liquidity provision, cross-pool arbitrage, regime conditioning, portfolio aggregation, and order flow); several apparent "edges" are a cost-on-persistence artifact of the shuffle, not alpha. (iv) Only one signal beats its null: a leakage-free cross-sectional machine-learning ranker on point-in-time features (out-of-sample rank-IC ≈0.06-0.08 at the 7-and 14-day horizons, labelpermutation p ≈ 0.005; insignificant at 30 days). We report it as a lead, not a result: its predictability is concentrated in the lower tail (it flags which coins crash, not which rise), every predicted decile's median forward return is negative, the long-only top-K edge is a winsorization-and-survivorship artifact, and it rests on only 15-30 disjoint rebalances. (v) Survivorship is the dominant uncontrolled threat to every cross-sectional result; a point-in-time, dead-pool-inclusive universe is reconstructable

title: Forecast Risk Premium
affiliations: DePaul University - Kellstadt Graduate School of Business and University of Illinois at Chicago - College of Business Administration

detail.title: Forecast Risk Premium
detail.abstract: We develop a model of analyst forecasts that explicitly accounts for state dependence in firm performance. The optimal published forecast equals a pricing-measure expectation rather than the physical conditional mean, generating a  "forecast risk premium." Consequently, even though analysts are compensated solely for accuracy under a symmetric loss function, their forecasts are downward-biased, with the magnitude of pessimism increasing in the firm's systematic risk. Consistent with this prediction and with prior evidence, earnings surprises relative to analyst forecasts are positive on average, with magnitudes that closely match a simple calibration of the model. We provide further support for the model using a battery of tests. First, surprises are positively related to market beta in the cross-section and to aggregate risk premia in the time-series. Second, these relations are driven by forecast bias rather than a positive association between beta and realized earnings. Third, analysts affiliated with brokerages with more cyclical hiring exhibit especially pronounced forecast pessimism. Finally, the forecast risk premium predicts announcement returns. We conclude that analyst forecasts embed risk premia and therefore do not represent unbiased expectations of firm performance.

title: Reconstructing 12-lead ECG from 3 leads with brief patient-specific calibration and comprehensive evaluation
affiliations: , Zhejiang University, Zhejiang University - College of Biomedical Engineering & Instrument Science and Zhejiang University

detail.title: Reconstructing 12-lead ECG from 3 leads with brief patient-specific calibration and comprehensive evaluation
detail.abstract: Reconstructing the full 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) from a reduced lead set is essential for continuous monitoring with wearable and patch devices, which can only acquire a few leads in practice. Existing deep-learning methods treat reconstruction as a generic signal-to-signal mapping and ignore patient-specific anatomical information obtainable through a brief 12-lead calibration acquisition at device setup. We propose CaLiNet-E, a calibration-aware framework combining per-patient ridge calibration, a quality-gated soft fallback, and a FiLM-conditioned non-linear residual network. We adopt a three-level evaluation framework: signal-level (Pearson correlation, normalised RMSE), feature-level (R-wave amplitude, ST-J+60 ms displacement, T-wave amplitude), and diagnostic-level (downstream macro F1 of pretrained 12-lead classifiers). On PTB-XL, CaLiNet-E achieves Pearson correlation 0.967, normalised RMSE 0.220, and ST-J+60 ms anterior error of 0.041 mV (a 2.4-fold safety margin to the 0.1 mV STEMI threshold). On out-of-distribution CPSC2018, CaLiNet-E preserves Pearson correlation 0.941. Diagnostic-level evaluation on two independent datasets shows macro F1 retention of 99.2% on PTB-XL fold 9 and statistically indistinguishable performance from the original signals on CODE-test. Comparing non-calibrated deep methods, adding a fixed population-level linear anchor markedly improves F1 retention while leaving Pearson correlation unchanged, highlighting the importance of clinically grounded linear priors for diagnostic fidelity.

title: Comparative Study Of Lecturers' Wellbeing In Public And Private Universities And Job Performance In Cross River State

detail.title: Comparative Study Of Lecturers' Wellbeing In Public And Private Universities And Job Performance In Cross River State

declarations.ethicsApproval: Approval consent was requested before involving participants
declarations.funderStatement: No funding for this research study

detail.abstract: This study examined the comparative differences in lecturers' wellbeing and job performance between public and private universities in Cross River State, Nigeria. Specifically, the study appraised five dimensions of lecturers' wellbeing employers' policy, workload, strike action, job security, and incentive package as predictors of job performance differentials across institutional types. Persistent poor job performance among university lecturers in Nigeria, manifesting in inadequate instructional delivery, limited research engagement, and recurrent industrial disputes, provided the empirical motivation for the inquiry. The study was grounded in Herzberg's Motivation Two-Factor Theory (1959) and Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs Theory (1943), and adopted a descriptive cross-sectional survey design. The target population comprised 2,471 lecturers and heads of departments from the University of Calabar (public) and Arthur Jarvis University (private) in Cross River State, from which a proportionate sample of 181 respondents was selected through the hat-and-draw and simple random sampling techniques. Data were collected using two researcher-developed instruments: the Lecturers' Wellbeing Questionnaire (LWQ, α = 0.86) and the Job Performance Questionnaire (JPQ, α = 0.84), both of which were validated by educational measurement experts. Research questions were addressed using independent samples t-test, while the five null hypotheses were tested at the 0.05 level of significance using one-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA), with post hoc comparisons conducted via Tukey's HSD. Findings revealed statistically significant inter-institutional differences across all five wellbeing dimensions in their relationship with job performance: employers' policy (F = 43.385, p = .000), lecturers' workload (F = 10.023, p = .003), strike action (F = 20.234, p = .000), job security (F = 11.085, p = .002), and incentive package (F = 21.593, p = .000). All five null hypotheses were consequently rejected. It was concluded that lecturers' wellbeing differs significantly between public and private universities in Cross River State, and that these differences exert a measurable influence on academic job performance. The study recommends that government and university management prioritise the formulation of lecturer-friendly institutional policies, recruit additional academic staff to alleviate workload burden, strengthen tenure and job security frameworks, and restructure incentive packages to adequately reflect lecturers' professional contributions, as prerequisite conditions for sustainable improvement in university-level instructional quality and academic output.

title: Complexity, Strategy, and Learning in Experimental Games
affiliations: Princeton University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Complexity, Strategy, and Learning in Experimental Games
detail.abstract: This paper studies how complexity shapes behavior in strategic environments. I conduct an experiment in which participants repeatedly play symmetric, normal-form games designed to vary in numerous features. Because game complexity is difficult to define theoretically, I develop an approach to synthesize multiple correlated proxies for complexity into a sparse, interpretable index. The index reveals that the effects of complexity due to the number of actions can be offset by equilibrium features of games, such as unique Pareto dominant outcomes. Providing participants with advance knowledge of opponents' strategies reduces complexity but does not eliminate it, suggesting that both strategic ambiguity and lottery complexity both influence game difficulty. Rather than inducing focal behavior, greater complexity leads strategies to become more dispersed in ways inconsistent with rational behavior. There is little evidence for learning in most games in the experiment, but initial feedback is most informative in highly complex games.

title: White Paper on Fairness in Music Ecosystems

detail.abstract:
The digitalisation of the music ecosystem has fundamentally reshaped how music is created, distributed, and monetised. A small number of platforms - including Spotify, YouTube, Apple Music, and TikTok - now operate as crucial intermediaries between artists and audiences, wielding significant algorithmic, data, and commercial power. While digital services have broadened access and stimulated new creative practices, they have also concentrated economic and informational power in ways that raise urgent questions of fairness in remuneration, visibility, participation, and governance.

This White Paper presents the findings and policy recommendations of Fair MusE (Promoting Fairness of the Music Ecosystem in a Platform-Dominated and Post-Pandemic Europe), a Horizon Europe project bringing together legal scholars, economists, and data scientists in ongoing dialogue with creators, collective management organisations, and policymakers. The paper identifies three interlocking sources of systemic imbalance: persistent barriers to fair remuneration and contractual parity for creators and smaller intermediaries, despite the rights introduced by the 2019 DSM Directive; pervasive data and algorithmic opacity that limits the ability of creators, researchers, and regulators to scrutinise the systems shaping cultural visibility and value; and institutional fragmentation across EU policy fields - from copyright and cultural policy to platform regulation and competition law - that weakens enforcement and inhibits a coherent European strategy.

The paper argues that metadata quality, interoperable data infrastructures, and algorithmic accountability are central preconditions for fairness, not secondary concerns. It further contends that fairness in the digital music ecosystem is fundamentally a governance challenge: digital markets do not merely distribute content, they shape cultural memory, linguistic plurality, and the conditions under which artistic work can flourish.

The policy recommendations integrate substantive creator rights under the DSM Directive, structural transparency obligations under the DSA and DMA, cultural diversity objectives under Article 167 TFEU and the UNESCO Convention on Cultural Diversity, and competition principles within a unified framework. Key proposals include strengthening copyright enforcement and harmonisation; embedding algorithmic transparency and accountability; establishing a European Music Data Space; creating a permanent EU Music Observatory; and developing fairness metrics and diversity-by-design standards for recommender systems.

Implemented together, these measures offer a practical roadmap for ensuring that Europe's digital transition enhances - rather than undermines - the sustainability, plurality, and richness of its cultural ecosystem.

title: From Farm Gate to Market Queen: Structural Drivers of Horticultural Postharvest Losses in Ghana

detail.title: From Farm Gate to Market Queen: Structural Drivers of Horticultural Postharvest Losses in Ghana
detail.abstract: Ghana's agricultural sector contributes approximately 20-21% of GDP and employs roughly 35% of the national workforce. Despite significant investment in crop production, a structural crisis continues to undermine agricultural gains: postharvest losses (PHLs) in the horticultural sub-sector covering tomatoes, peppers, leafy vegetables, and other perishable crops are estimated at 30-50% of total annual production. These losses translate to an estimated $295-385 million in foregone revenue each year from the horticultural sub-sector alone, threatening national food security, smallholder livelihoods, and Ghana's broader agro-industrialization agenda. The core structural constraint is a near-total absence of integrated, reliable, and affordable cold chain infrastructure connecting smallholder farmers to domestic markets and export channels. The result is a system characterized by excessive field-to-market transit times, inadequate storage, poor packaging, and negligible access to refrigerated logistics conditions that accelerate microbial spoilage, mechanical damage, and physiological deterioration of produce. This paper adopts a systematic review methodology, combining a structured review of peer reviewed literature and institutional reports on postharvest losses (PHLs) in Ghana and comparable Sub-Saharan African contexts, a secondary-data value chain analysis of the tomato and pepper supply corridors, stakeholder mapping of actors from farm to final market, and a comparative analysis of cold chain policy interventions in Kenya, Ethiopia, and South Africa. The paper finds that PHLs are not primarily a technology problem but a governance and investment coordination failure: market incentives are misaligned, public investment has been fragmented and underfunded, extension services inadequately cover postharvest handling, and smallholder farmers cannot individually bear the capital cost of cold chain infrastructure. Building on these findings, the paper proposes a five-pillar National Postharvest Cold Chain Policy Framework (NPCCPF): a dedicated National Postharvest Development Fund (NPDF), a district-level Community Cold Hubs (CCHs) network across high-production districts, mandatory postharvest handling standards and their enforcement, an integrated postharvest extension framework, and public-private partnerships (PPPs) for refrigerated logistics and agro-processing linkages. The framework is designed to produce measurable reductions in horticultural PHLs, expand agro-logistics employment, and improve farmgate prices for targeted commodities.

title: Germany’s Economic Crossroads: Stagnation, Structural Challenges and Policy Reponses

detail.title: Germany’s Economic Crossroads: Stagnation, Structural Challenges and Policy Reponses
detail.abstract: Germany, recognized as the economic powerhouse of Europe with a gross domestic product (GDP) of 4,305 billion euros in 2024, is recently facing persistent economic stagnation. While other nations in Europe have reported a remarkable 5% growth in GDP, Germanys performance remains sluggish, particularly due to series of economic burdens and structural challenges (Glunz & von Prittwitz, 2023). Several economic burdens contributed to its downturn. The Covid-19 pandemic triggered logistics disruptions and labor shortages, straining the industry resources and productions. The high energy prices exacerbated by geopolitical conflicts (Russia-Ukraine war) increased inflation, impacting both consumers and corporations. Additionally, Germanys high reliance on China exports backfired, pulling down one of the biggest sources of income, exports and trades especially in automobile industry. Escalating demographic challenges such as aging population and declining workforce are further deepening the crisis. Such erratic situations have led to a vicious circle of turbulent instability and financial fragility in recent years leading to a 4.58% decline in GDP (2022) (initial impact of crisis). It has been challenging traditional business frameworks and compelling businesses to adjust their production process (DIW Berlin: German Economy Currently Scarcely Making Headway, 2023). Even though Germany is the third largest economy in the world, such headwinds can lead Germany into a recession if they are not being addressed. Therefore, this report empirically evaluates the economic situation of Germany, its impact on key stake holders and the effectiveness of governments response to stabilize the economy henceforth, providing an outline to navigate the challenges and ensure economic long-term sustainability

title: Auxiliary Benefits and the Fiscal Sustainability of Social Security in an Aging Economy
affiliations: Otaru University of Commerce

detail.title: Auxiliary Benefits and the Fiscal Sustainability of Social Security in an Aging Economy
detail.abstract: This paper studies the impact of auxiliary benefits on the sustainability of Social Security in an aging economy. I develop a computable overlapping generations model with heterogeneous households in which individuals may be single or married, face marriage and divorce risks, and may become widowed, thereby explicitly incorporating auxiliary benefits into the analysis. Using the calibrated model, I simulate an aging economy to quantify the additional taxes required to sustain the Social Security system. The results show that auxiliary benefits significantly increase the fiscal burden and that the gap in required taxes between economies with and without auxiliary benefits widens as the population ages. This gap remains substantial even when the retirement age is raised. The analysis provides quantitative insights into the macroeconomic and fiscal effects of auxiliary benefits. Moreover, incorporating marriage and divorce risks is essential; otherwise, the fiscal impact of auxiliary benefits is overstated.

title: Brief of Amicus Curiae Dr. Ron D. Katznelson in Support of Affirmance in Microsoft Corp. v. i4i Limited Partnership, US Supreme Court Case No. 10-290
affiliations: Bi-Level Technologies

detail.title: Brief of Amicus Curiae Dr. Ron D. Katznelson in Support of Affirmance in Microsoft Corp. v. i4i Limited Partnership, US Supreme Court Case No. 10-290

keywords: proof by clear and convincing evidence

detail.abstract:
Civil cases involving litigants having countervailing interests of substantial disparity, prescribe the heightened standard of proof as a “default.” In re Winship, 397 U.S. 358, 371 (1970) (Harlan, J., concurring); Santosky v. Kramer, 455 U.S. 745, 758 (1982). The substantial disparity in the countervailing risks of loss in patent invalidity proceedings leads to the “default” heightened standard of proof which has been applied in patent law for more than 150 years.

The fundamental principle that governs the standard of proof generally under this Court’s jurisprudence involves allocating the risk of factfinder errors between the litigants in a manner that reflects their relative expected risk (harm in the event of an error). Addington v. Texas 441 U.S. 418, 423 (1979). Thus, a higher burden of proof will be required for a verdict against the litigant that will suffer harm that is substantially greater than that suffered by the adverse litigant under erroneous decisions. The degree of asymmetry in the countervailing risks to the litigants determines the standard of proof. Symmetry of the risks among litigants – where both parties have equal risks – creates the ‘preponderance of the evidence’ standard; high asymmetry corresponds to the ‘clear and convincing evidence’ standard; and extremely high asymmetry corresponds to the ‘beyond reasonable doubt’ standard, often used in criminal law.

In contrast with infringement adjudication errors where the litigants face comparable risks, the countervailing risks of error in patent invalidity proceedings are vastly different in magnitude for each litigant. Whereas the alleged infringer’s risk in an adverse decision amounts only to damages incurred by his own infringing activity, the patentee’s risk under an error against him is that of losing the patent rights altogether, losing recovery not only from the alleged infringer but from all other parties. Under such errors, the patentee would be unlikely to receive returns on investments made in discovery and development of the invention – investments made in reliance on the patent bargain. In addition, when the factfinder erroneously invalidates the patent, the patentee suffers irreparable harm brought about by the public disclosure of the invention required in exchange for the patent grant. (The accused infringer and the public are unjustly enriched). Thus, the quid pro quo of the patent bargain transfers much of the risk of loss to the patentee – a risk not sustained by other parties.

Therefore, the patent bargain and the associated highly asymmetric risks that it imparts on the parties command the “default” heightened standard of proof that apply under this Court’s precedents. This requirement does not originate from the patent statute. Rather, it is based on immutable legal principles rooted in traditional American jurisprudence as reaffirmed in Winship and Santosky – prescribing unconditionally heightened standard of proof whenever the magnitude of the countervailing interests of the litigants are highly asymmetric. Such is the case in patent invalidity proceedings.

The heightened standard of proof operates regardless of whether or not administrative deference to PTO examination is due. It is an inevitable result grounded in the fundamental principles in Winship and Santosky. As shown in Section V, because these principles have long been a legal tradition, the heightened standard of proof appears to have prevailed even before the PTO started examining patent applications in 1836. Petitioner provides no evidence that a preponderance of evidence standard existed prior to 1836, when the U.S. was operating a patent registration system. Rather, despite the lower confidence the public had in the validity of patents, evidence provided in Section V suggests that during that time the courts had nevertheless conducted adjudications in a manner consistent with the heightened standard.

The heightened standard in the presumption of validity is therefore a basic doctrine of the patent bargain which produces substantial disparity in the countervailing risks of error. The presumption is established when the PTO grants the patent, whether or not the PTO examined it for novelty, non-anticipation, or non-obviousness. Congress’ enactment of PTO examination procedures in 1836 was aimed not at establishing the presumption of validity but rather at further justifying its existence. For the reasons stated above and further elaborated below, the Federal Circuit’s judgment should be affirmed.

title: MediaWiki Code2Code Search: Neural Retrieval for the Semantic Discovery of Open-Source Software Entities
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: MediaWiki Code2Code Search: Neural Retrieval for the Semantic Discovery of Open-Source Software Entities
detail.abstract: Code search in large-scale ecosystems is often hindered by the lexical gap between user queries and implementation details, alongside the trade-off between the low latency of traditional Information Retrieval (IR) and the precision of Deep Learning (DL). We present MediaWiki Code2Code Search, a neural retrieval system for semantic code-to-code discovery. By indexing 1.29 million structural entities (functions, types, and templates) across 2,500+ MediaWiki repositories, our system enables retrieval based on computational intent rather than surface tokens. We employ a split-build architecture, decoupling GPU-intensive offline indexing from a CPU-only serving layer; our FAISS IVF-PQ index occupies 168.6 MB: a 96.6\% reduction compared to a flat float32 baseline, and achieves a median query latency of 1.85 seconds on commodity hardware, satisfying the 6 GiB RAM constraint of Wikimedia Toolforge. Our evaluation across a 27-query benchmark demonstrates superior performance over the BM25 baseline, achieving a P@10 of 0.87 compared to 0.64 (0.52 versus 0.34 for strict matching). Gains are most pronounced in name-obfuscated tasks where lexical methods fail. The system is available at code2codesearch.toolforge.org under the Apache 2.0 licence and provides an open RESTful API.

title: Bodies in the Beds: How REITs, Private Equity Firms, and County Hospitals Monetize Nursing Home Residents as Real Estate Acquisitions
affiliations: University of Baltimore - School of Law

detail.title: Bodies in the Beds: How REITs, Private Equity Firms, and County Hospitals Monetize Nursing Home Residents as Real Estate Acquisitions

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Baltimore School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Baltimore School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Nursing home residents have become monetized targets of real estate acquisitions. Established in 1960, Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) were envisioned as allowing individuals to invest in commercial real estate without owning properties. That seemingly innocuous investment idea has led to the growth of a behind-the-scenes empire of little-understood conglomerates of REITs buying up nursing homes and other healthcare facilities across the country. Capitalizing on tax-exempt income incentives, exploiting “triple-net” leasebacks, funneling profits through subsidiaries, and shielding ownership and assets from the liability of operations, the corporatized owners extract cash from facilities and leave harm in their wake. And to grow the extractive operations, individuals and corporations can often invest in REITs on the stock market, lured with dividends siphoned from the “silver tsunami” of aging humans.

REITs are not alone, as private equity (PE) firms of every size have also set their sights on nursing homes. Further, local government hospital systems in multiple states are now mimicking private profiteering by similarly buying up nursing homes, not to improve care, but to take their Medicaid funds for other uses. The acquisition strategies of REITs, PE firms, and county hospital systems vary in structure, but they all share a common commodification need: bodies in the beds—maximizing occupancy rates while minimizing money spent on care—to increase the cash siphoned away.

This Article maps the maze of parasitic nursing home acquisition, revenue strategies, and resulting concerns, concluding with a call to curtail the practices—to convert the harm into care.

title: The role of educational interventions in eliminating knowledge barriers to energy efficiency in young people: Evidence from a Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT) in Nepal
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and ETH Zürich - CER-ETH - Center of Economic Research at ETH Zurich

detail.title: The role of educational interventions in eliminating knowledge barriers to energy efficiency in young people: Evidence from a Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT) in Nepal
detail.abstract: In this study, we evaluate the impact of a short classroom-based educational intervention designed to improve financial literacy, energy-related financial literacy, and sustainability literacy among high school students in Nepal. The analysis is based on the primary data obtained from a randomized controlled trial (RCT) with 1,320 high school students in Kathmandu. The results reveal significant effects of the treatment leading to substantial improvement (short-run) in combined literacy scores (sum of energy-related financial literacy and sustainability literacy) by 7.86 points (175% increase), application skills by 1.73 points (89%), and the probability of choosing an energy-efficient motorbike in a hypothetical scenario increased by 24.7 percentage points (65%). Mediation analysis, used to examine potential channels of impact, indicates that 73% of the choice of the energy-efficient motorbike is driven by improved computational skills. These results provide robust evidence that brief educational interventions can effectively close knowledge barriers and potentially narrow intention-behavior gaps. These insights offer an avenue for further research and policy instigation to promote energy-efficient consumption in developing countries.

title: An Updated Estimate of the Size of Malta's Underground Economy
affiliations: Central Bank of Malta

detail.title: An Updated Estimate of the Size of Malta's Underground Economy

publicationDetails.detailsText: Central Bank of Malta Research Paper Series No. 06/2026
publicationDetails.journalName: Central Bank of Malta Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: The underground, or shadow, economy – comprising legal and productive activities concealed from authorities for monetary, regulatory, or institutional reasons – poses challenges to fiscal governance, labour protection, and market competition. This paper provides an updated estimate of the size of Malta’s underground economy over the period 1995–2024, employing a Multiple Indicators and Multiple Causes (MIMIC) model estimated on quarterly data. The specification includes four causal variables (tax burden, government expenditure, self-employment, and unemployment) and three indicators (currency-to-GDP ratio, real GDP growth, and labour force participation). All variables except government expenditure are statistically significant and display the expected signs. Increases in the tax burden, self-employment, and unemployment are associated with higher shadow-economy activity. The estimated trajectory of the shadow economy over the sample period suggests that the underground economy’s share of GDP rose modestly until 2009 and declined thereafter, reaching 15.3% in 2024. The findings are robust to alternative specifications and consistent with the empirical tendency for informality to decline with economic growth, as well as with increased institutional capacity focused on reducing tax evasion and other aspects of the informal economy in Malta.

title: Persistent Spatial Inequalities in Contraceptive Use in Nigeria: A Bayesian Spatio-Temporal model Evidence from Demographic Health Survey Data from 2003 to 2024
affiliations: University of Abuja, University of Abuja and University of Abuja

detail.title: Persistent Spatial Inequalities in Contraceptive Use in Nigeria: A Bayesian Spatio-Temporal model Evidence from Demographic Health Survey Data from 2003 to 2024

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received from anywhere.

detail.abstract:
Introduction: Contraceptive use remains unevenly distributed across Nigeria despite ongoing reproductive health interventions. This study assessed the spatio-temporal distribution and determinants of contraceptive use among women of reproductive age in Nigeria.

Methods: Data from the 2003, 2008, 2013, 2018, and 2024 Nigeria Demographic and Health Surveys involving 127,865 women aged 15-49 years were analyzed. Bayesian spatio-temporal conditional autoregressive models were fitted using the Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA) approach. Spatial, temporal, and nonlinear effects were modeled, and posterior exceedance probabilities were estimated.

Results: Overall prevalence of contraceptive use increased from 14.5% in 2003 to 20.7% in 2024, with a pooled prevalence of 16.0%. Contraceptive use was significantly associated with education ([[EQUATION]] = 13192.019, p<0.001) also wealth index, residence, marital status, and region were all significantly associated with increase prevalence of contraceptive use. Women with higher education had over four times higher odds of contraceptive use (OR = 4.10; 95%CI: 3.79-4.43), while women from the richest households had significantly higher odds of use (OR = 2.78; 95% CI: 2.55-3.03). Significant spatial heterogeneity persisted across states (σ=0.54), with southern states showing higher exceedance probabilities of contraceptive prevalence above the national average.

Conclusion: Although contraceptive use improved over time, substantial spatial and socioeconomic inequalities remain across Nigeria. Targeted reproductive health interventions should prioritize underserved northern and rural communities to reduce persistent disparities in contraceptive use.

detail.abstract: U.S. trade policy stands at a critical inflection point. While the Biden administration’s “worker-centered” approach and the Trump administration’s “America First” platform sharply diverge, both recognize that trade deeply impacts domestic employment. However, both policies overlook how the treatment and costs of labor in partner nations directly protect U.S. workers from unfair competition. This Article argues that empowering foreign trade-sector workers to secure higher wages and better conditions must become a central pillar of U.S. trade policy. Drawing on an original empirical study of Mexico’s automotive sector under the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA), I demonstrate that recent "worker-centered" efforts failed to truly empower foreign labor. Instead, they left workers vulnerable, incentivized corporate offshoring, and suppressed foreign consumer power—deficiencies that ultimately harmed domestic workers and fueled protectionist, tariff-driven alternatives. By uncovering the direct link between foreign supply-chain capacity and U.S. job opportunities, this Article challenges conventional narratives surrounding trade agreements and foreign aid. Ultimately, it underscores the urgent need to radically reconceptualize U.S. trade policy to protect the global workers who make trade possible.
