detail.abstract:
This paper presents and considers a simple efficient new way or mechanism, mainly using basic applied mathematics, to tweak the current UK House of Commons  (HoC) parliamentary system so that its current and very long established 1st Past the Post (1PP) MP election system, and MP parliamentary voting system, can also be made fully or partly reflective of national voting Proportional Representation (PR).

The model below is of very general application and can be applied to any 1PP election system for national representatives like MPs and any net majority voting system like the HoC.

The proposed new system would be very low cost to implement in practice although could have a dramatic effect on MP parliamentary voting and government outcomes and help provide much better alignment between underlying citizen preferences and desires and HoC vote results.

title: Gödel's Disjunction, Non-Ergodicity and the Limits of Theoretical Psychology: Some Reflections on the Hayek-Turing-Gödel Connection

detail.title: Gödel's Disjunction, Non-Ergodicity and the Limits of Theoretical Psychology: Some Reflections on the Hayek-Turing-Gödel Connection
detail.abstract: This paper constitutes an attempt to clarify certain tensions and unresolved issues in Hayek’s theory of mind, in particular from the perspective of the possibilities and potentialities, but also the limitations of general machine intelligence. The main question examined in this paper relates to the possibility of general machine intelligence (AGI) from the perspective of Hayek’s theoretical psychology as developed mainly in The Sensory Order. This question was also famously raised by Turing which raises questions regarding the nature of a possible Hayek-Turing conjunction or even connection. A few further connections have to be considered, however, in particular with Gödel and von Neumann. The scientific-cognitive and philosophical value of Hayek’s The Sensory Order has been assessed in divergent ways by different authors and with varying degrees of perspicacity. Hayek’s suggestion concerning the possibility of general machine intelligence following the principles of his theoretical psychology is problematic and must be considered an anomaly in his theoretical system.

title: Environmental, Climate, and Economic Aspects of Dairy Cow Farming
affiliations: National Research Institute - Institute of Agricultural and Food Economics - National Research Institute (IAFE-NRI), National Research Institute - Institute of Agricultural and Food Economics - National Research Institute (IAFE-NRI), National Research Institute (PIB) - Institute of Agricultural and Food Economics - National Research Institute (IAFE-NRI), National Research Institute - Institute of Agricultural and Food Economics - National Research Institute (IAFE-NRI) and National Research Institute (PIB) - Institute of Agricultural and Food Economics - National Research Institute (IAFE-NRI)

detail.title: Environmental, Climate, and Economic Aspects of Dairy Cow Farming
detail.abstract: The aim of the research was to determine the significance of cattle farming (especially dairy cows) in the use of forage area, mainly permanent grassland, and its relationship with the natural environment in terms of greenhouse gas emissions (methane), water consumption, and biodiversity. The analysis concerned 1,823 dairy farms under observation of the Polish FADN between 2018 and 2020 and managed by natural persons. The following aspects were taken into account: production potential of farms, production and economic results, organization of plant and animal production depending on the structure of forage area determined by the share of permanent grassland in the area. It was found that the production potential of the dairy farms under consideration and their production and economic results were negatively correlated with increased share of permanent grassland in the forage area. It was also found that a higher share of permanent grassland in the forage area: meant a higher share of valuable nature area in the farm; was specifically correlated with the balance of organic matter in the soil; the balance was positive in all of the considered cases, i.e., they kept an increasing amount of water in the soil and increasing amounts of carbon dioxide each year; resulted in a significant increase in water consumption per 1 liter of milk produced, but the situation was related to increased share of permanent grassland in the forage area and lower milk yield of cows.

title: Organic Farming in the European Union in the Face of the Challenges of Sustainable Consumption
affiliations: University of Lodz

detail.title: Organic Farming in the European Union in the Face of the Challenges of Sustainable Consumption
detail.abstract: The aim of the study is to present the link between organic farming and sustainable consumption in the light of the European Green Deal strategy (EGD). The article discusses whether the increase in the supply of organic food and the solutions proposed in the strategy will contribute to the spread of sustainable consumption. The article was prepared based on a critical analysis of the literature based on available statistical data, strategic documents, and scientific studies. The paper uses desk research and secondary data from Eurostat, FAOStat, and IFOAM for European Union countries (EU) between 2014 and 2020. It has been found that the implementation of the principles of sustainable consumption through organic farming requires action to increase consumers' confidence in organic food products. The credibility of organic farming must be built at every stage of the supply chain. From the perspective of achieving the principles of sustainable consumption and production through the development of organic farming, it is important to ensure a reliable certification system at every stage of the supply chain and labeling that takes into account detailed information about the product. Public procurement, which could generate sustainable demand for organic food products, is the development opportunity for organic farming. The analysis showed that the actions and tools identified in the European Green Deal strategy, within the framework of the three main priorities, appear to be legitimate and crucial for the development of organic agriculture and market for organic food products.

title: A Comparison between Official Measurement and Individual Perspectives on Disability: Investigation into Disability Statistics in Indonesia
affiliations: , University of Southampton and University of Southampton

detail.title: A Comparison between Official Measurement and Individual Perspectives on Disability: Investigation into Disability Statistics in Indonesia

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests. There are no personal or financial relationships with individuals or organisations that could be perceived to have influenced the design, analysis, or reporting of this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethical approval was granted by the University of Southampton Ethics and Research Governance Committee (ERGO: 80952.A1). Permission was obtained from Statistics Indonesia (BPS) as the survey commissioner for SUSENAS, and the Ministry of Health Indonesia (KEMENKES) as the survey commissioner for RISKESDAS and the provider of the linked data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded by the Economic and Social Research Council South Coast Doctoral Training Partnership (ES/P000673/1).

detail.abstract: This study addresses significant gaps in official disability statistics. Despite efforts by international bodies, such as the UNCRPD and WHO, to improve disability data collection, the official statistics often fail to reflect the true experiences of individuals with disabilities in Indonesia. This study examines the gap between official disability classifications and a more inclusive measurement approach. Through a mixed-methods approach, this study utilises both secondary quantitative data from two nationally representative cross-sectional surveys in Indonesia in 2018, the National Socio-Economic Survey (SUSENAS), conducted by Statistics Indonesia (BPS), and the National Basic Health Research (RISKESDAS), conducted by the Ministry of Health (KEMENKES), and primary qualitative data from in-depth interviews with people with disabilities and their families. Initial findings reveal a substantial decline in reported disability prevalence from 2.8% to 15.2%, which raises questions about data accuracy. Interviews with participants highlight issues such as misclassification and the inadequacy of existing survey questions in capturing the nuanced experiences of disability. This study proposes developing new, context-specific measurement tools that better reflect the lived realities of people with disabilities in Indonesia by integrating the voices of the people into the current discussion of disability measurement. Working closely with those who have experienced disability and whose opinions are the most valuable further emphasises that this research is done with them and not just about them.

title: Direct and Indirect Consequences of the War in Ukraine for Polish Trade in Agri-Food Products
affiliations: Independent and  Institute of Central Europe

detail.title: Direct and Indirect Consequences of the War in Ukraine for Polish Trade in Agri-Food Products
detail.abstract: The ongoing war in Ukraine is associated with a number of negative and long-term macroeconomic consequences for Poland and other countries both in the area of trade and maintaining supply chains, as well as the security of energy supplies. Many entities in the agri-food sector are affected by this impact. The aim of the article is to assess the effects of the war in Ukraine on Polish agri-food trade. The paper presents the production and trade potential of Ukraine, defines trends in Polish agri-food trade with Ukraine after February 24, 2022, and identifies the main effects for Polish agri-food trade resulting from the ongoing armed conflict in Ukraine. Several research methods were used in the article, ranging from a literature review and document analysis, through a statistical and descriptive method of production and trade data analysis, to competitiveness indices: the index of comparative advantages (RCA) and trade coverage ratio (TC). The research shows that in 2022 Polish imports of agri-food products from Ukraine increased almost three times in terms of value, as compared to 2021, reaching EUR 2.8 billion, which increased the competitive pressure on the internal market. It has also been proven that only part of agri-food products imported from Ukraine is subject to mutual Polish-Ukrainian competition on the EU market. This applies to products such as wheat, poultry meat, birds' eggs, frozen fruit, but also highly processed food products, including confectionery and pastry. Further development of trade in agri-food products with Ukraine will be determined primarily by the situation at the front, the supply of goods for export, the possibility of exporting Ukrainian goods through the Black Sea ports, and the permeability of land solidarity routes. Data shows that in 2022 the yields of cereals, legumes, and oilseeds in Ukraine decreased by 34%, which should also translate into decreased exports.

title: Informal Economy and Agricultural Productivity in Bangladesh: A Time Series Analysis
affiliations: Mawlana Bhashani Science and Technology University and Mawlana Bhashani Science and Technology University

detail.title: Informal Economy and Agricultural Productivity in Bangladesh: A Time Series Analysis
detail.abstract: The aim of the study was to investigate the relationship between the informal economy and agricultural productivity in Bangladesh over a 25-year period from 1993 to 2018. While the impact of the black market on the economy is a well-studied topic, its implications for the agricultural sector in this specific country context was less explored. By controlling structural transformation, trade, and foreign direct investment (FDI) in agriculture, the authors employ autoregressive distributed lag (ARDL) using Kripfganz and Schneider's (2018) approximations, as well as fully modified ordinary least square (FMOLS) and feasible generalized least square (FGLS) techniques. The results reveal that informality initially hampers agricultural productivity in the short term due to reduced government revenue, but in the long run, it acts as an active social protection system, fostering informal employment and providing essential amenities. Although the study's time span limits the investigation to this specific period, it serves as a crucial attempt to assess the impact of informality on agriculture in Bangladesh, highlighting the need for cautious consideration of both the benefits and drawbacks of the informal sector in enhancing agricultural productivity. Policymakers in Bangladesh should act cautiously, acknowledging the nuances of the informal sector's influence on agriculture to leverage its potential for sustainable economic growth.

title: Multi-Temporal Satellite Assessment of Drought Severity and Land Use Dynamics in Sudan, White Nile, Eldoueim Locality
affiliations: Higher Council for Environment and Natural Resources and University of Khartoum - Institute of Environmental Studies

detail.title: Multi-Temporal Satellite Assessment of Drought Severity and Land Use Dynamics in Sudan, White Nile, Eldoueim Locality

declarations.ethicsApproval: this research deals with monitoring natural resource changes using remote sensing

detail.abstract: This study analyzes drought severity, vegetation dynamics, and land use/land cover (LULC) changes in Eldouiem locality, Sudan, using multi-temporal Landsat imagery (1985, 1995, 2015, and 2022). Remote sensing indices-Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), Normalized Difference Water Index (NDWI), and Normalized Difference Drought Index (NDDI)-were applied to evaluate vegetation health, water stress, and drought intensity. Supervised classification with Support Vector Machine (SVM) was used to generate LULC maps. Results reveal a marked intensification of drought severity. Moderate severity declined sharply from 55.9% in 1985 to 16.1% in 2022, while very high severity expanded from 0.8% to 37.5%. NDVI analysis showed initial vegetation improvement in 1995, followed by decline in 2015-2022, particularly in southeastern zones. LULC results highlight significant transformations: agriculture expanded from 4.3% to 15.7%, settlements grew from 8.4% to 41.3%, while rangelands declined from 35% to 29.5%, and forests shrank from 0.7% to 0.2%. Bare lands decreased drastically from 49% to 10%. These findings demonstrate that Eldouiem has undergone intensifying drought stress, vegetation decline, and rapid land use change, underscoring the need for integrated drought monitoring and sustainable land management strategies.

title: Generalized Physically-Consistent Kernel Density Estimation with Limited Grouped Data Contamination
affiliations: Johns Hopkins University

detail.title: Generalized Physically-Consistent Kernel Density Estimation with Limited Grouped Data Contamination

keywords: Fredholm Integral Equation of the Second Kind

detail.abstract: This paper treats the deconvolution model Y = SX1 + (1-S) k j=1 Xj where k is a known integer satisfying k ≥ 2, S has a known Bernoulli distribution with P [S = 1] ∈ (0, 1), and (X1, ..., X k) are I.I.D. from a distribution having Lebesgue density fX. The aim is to estimate fX using observations from Y. A prominent application arises in finance, where high-frequency asset returns do not always exclusively reflect current news due to information lags. Unlike the classic grouped data deconvolution model where P [S = 1] = 0 (Meister 2007), this estimation problem is well-posed provided P [S = 1] is large enough. This substantially reduces the difficulty of the estimation problem. The proposed estimator has a Mean Integrated Square Error (MISE) converging at a rate which is equal to the optimal nonparametric rate of Fan (1993) without data grouping (i.e. if P [S = 1] = 1). Moreover, if the distribution of S is unknown, then a feasible estimator is proposed if the first moment of X is known or else if Xj represents the lag of order j-1 for some stationary process. The feasible estimator has an Integrated Square Error (ISE) which enjoys the same rate of convergence in probability. The methodology is easy to implement from data using a single tuning parameter. A Monte Carlo experiment reveals good finite-sample properties for the proposed estimator.

title:
Capital-Accumulation-Based Effective Demand
A Framework for Fiscal Policy, Purchasing Power, Asset-Entry Barriers, and Cost Pass-through
affiliations: Independent

detail.title:
Capital-Accumulation-Based Effective Demand
A Framework for Fiscal Policy, Purchasing Power, Asset-Entry Barriers, and Cost Pass-through
detail.abstract: This paper extends the concept of effective demand by distinguishing temporary nominal effective demand from durable capital-accumulation-based effective demand. Effective demand is commonly understood as demand backed by the ability and willingness to pay. This paper argues that such demand must also be evaluated across time: temporary nominal effective demand becomes durable effective demand only when it is supported by capital-accumulation capacity. Fiscal transfers, wage increases, and public expenditure can create immediate nominal demand, but they may fail to preserve real purchasing power if households cannot convert additional income into capital before asset and consumer prices adjust. The paper develops two purchasing-power paradoxes. First, fiscal expansion may raise nominal income among lower-income households, but if the additional income is absorbed by essential consumption, it may not become savings or assets. Meanwhile, liquidity expansion may raise asset prices and increase asset-entry barriers before these households can accumulate capital. Second, wage increases and broader infrastructure-cost increases may be intended to restore purchasing power, but if such costs are embedded repeatedly across production, logistics, distribution, services, financing, administration, and compliance chains, cumulative pass-through may raise final consumer prices and reduce real purchasing power. The framework formalizes liquidity dilution, effective-demand barriers, temporary effective demand, durable effective demand, consumption absorption, cumulative cost pass-through, and capital-accumulation capacity. It proposes a Median-Anchored Ladder Dividend System as an institutional mechanism for converting transfer-based temporary demand into capitalaccumulation-based durable effective demand. Under this system, citizens receive public asset claims such as sovereign wealth fund units, inflation-linked public bonds, diversified public fund units, or restricted capital-formation accounts. A base yield provides broad asset inclusion. A median-proximity supplement rewards structural settlement near the middle-income zone, while a wage-growth supplement rewards upward movement toward that zone. The median anchor is not intended as arbitrary favoritism toward the middle-income group. It is used as a macroeconomic stability anchor. A broad middle-income settlement zone can stabilize aggregate demand, reduce fiscal fragility, and lower social costs. The wage-growth supplement is designed to encourage work incentives among lower-income households, reduce dependency-based moral hazard, and transform part of social expenditure from repetitive consumption relief into capital formation. The revised yield structure also includes a social-cost-reduction supplement. This supplement recognizes that, especially in an AI-driven economy where traditional employment may become less abundant or structurally transformed, capital accumulation can also be linked to verified contributions that reduce public and social costs. Essential survival support remains protected. The contribution of the paper is conceptual. It does not reject Keynesian effective demand; rather, it extends the concept by adding time, asset-entry barriers, capital-accumulation capacity, and the social-cost dimension of incentive design. The central issue is not only 1 whether policy creates demand in the nominal sense, but whether it creates durable effective demand through capital accumulation before asset and consumer prices adjust.

title: The Tariff Stick and the Nationalist Rally: How the US-China Trade War Fuels Emotional Nationalism
affiliations: , Hunan University and Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST)

detail.title: The Tariff Stick and the Nationalist Rally: How the US-China Trade War Fuels Emotional Nationalism
detail.abstract: The U.S.-China trade war represents a consequential shock to the contemporary international economic order, yet its domestic political repercussions in China remain understudied. Leveraging approximately 6.5 million Weibo posts from 2012 to 2022, annotated with large language models, we operationalize nationalism through a 2 x 2 typology crossing inward versus outward orientation with emotional versus reasoned expression, yielding four forms: emotional patriotism, rational patriotism, emotional hostility, and rational hostility. We aggregate these measures to the city level and combine them with a shift-share measure of tariff exposure, showing that greater exposure increases emotional patriotism and emotional hostility while leaving the rational forms unchanged or diminished. Further analysis reveals that citizens in more exposed areas grow increasingly skeptical of American democracy and shift away from the iPhone, a salient symbol of American technology, toward Chinese brands.

title: Institutions Meet Individual Investors: Resolution of Uncertainty in the Equity Market
affiliations: Sabanci University, Georgetown University - McDonough School of Business, Sabanci University and Sveriges Riksbank - Research Division

detail.title: Institutions Meet Individual Investors: Resolution of Uncertainty in the Equity Market
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the cross-sectional predictive power of uncertainty for future equity returns, drawing a fundamental distinction between systematic and firm-specific uncertainty. We model the equity market with two types of investors: sophisticated institutional investors who trade rationally by exploiting mispricing, and naive retail investors who overweight the probability and severity of salient tail events. Using the U.S. 13F institutional/hedge fund holdings and Sweden household-level data, we find a significantly negative relation between future stock returns and both systematic and firm-specific uncertainty and show that systematic (firm-specific) uncertainty premium is more pronounced in stocks predominantly held by institutional (retail) investors.

title: Forecasting Crypto Volatility and Cross-Asset Correlations Using Aave v2 and v3 On-Chain Signals
affiliations: and Academy of Economic Studies Bucharest

detail.title: Forecasting Crypto Volatility and Cross-Asset Correlations Using Aave v2 and v3 On-Chain Signals
detail.abstract: This paper investigates whether variables associated with the leading decentralized finance (DeFi) lending protocol Aave exert measurable effects on the volatilities of Ethereum (ETH) and Bitcoin (BTC), as well as on their dynamic correlations with the S&P 500. We construct a dataset spanning January 2021 to December 2025, covering both Aave V2 and V3, from which we derive explanatory variables including utilization ratios, supply and borrowing rates and measures of pool-level lending risk. Principal component analysis (PCA) is applied to address dimensionality and multicollinearity, yielding two economically interpretable signals: a crypto inflow component capturing risk appetite, and a stablecoin inflow component consistent with flight-to-safety behavior. Cryptocurrency volatilities are computed using the Garman–Klass (GK) range-based estimator while dynamic cross-asset correlations are recovered via the Dynamic Conditional Correlation (DCC) framework. Granger causality tests and ARDL regression models reveal that the Aave risk appetite signal predicts changes in ETH GK volatility at lags 1 and 5 and dynamic correlations at all lags, with weaker effects on BTC volatility. Secondly, we observe a robust negative cumulative effect on all three dynamic correlations, indicating that expansions in DeFi activity systematically dampen crypto–equity co-movements and also lead to a decoupling of BTC and ETH. These results are robust to different volatility specifications and suggest that on-chain DeFi data contains forward-looking information and can help reduce parameter estimation risk, a critical issue in deriving optimal portfolios involving digital assets. We expect that DeFi protocol-level signals will become a standard component of empirical work on digital-asset pricing and risk.

title: Corporations as City Planners
affiliations: Albany Law School

detail.title: Corporations as City Planners
detail.abstract:
Under current law, large, publicly-backed development projects are often driven by private businesses. While not necessarily new, the main rationales for this approach are the demand elected officials face to deliver jobs, perceptions about failed public city planning, and the growing power of corporations relative to the diminished power of cities. title: Thermodynamic Waste, Health Capital, and Long-Run Growth: A Thermo-Ecological Augmentation of the Solow Model
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Thermodynamic Waste, Health Capital, and Long-Run Growth: A Thermo-Ecological Augmentation of the Solow Model
detail.abstract: This paper develops a thermo-ecological augmentation of the Solow growth model that treats production as a physical throughput process generating both useful output and unavoidable thermodynamic waste. We introduce three coupled state variables absent from the standard framework: (i) physical thermodynamic output (TO), the energy waste, emissions, and material inefficiency created as a byproduct of production, valued at shadow prices derived from the social cost of carbon and analogous pollutant valuations; (ii) health capital (H), a stock variable linking pollution exposure to effective labor supply, cognitive performance, and total factor productivity; and (iii) natural capital (R), resource stocks subject to depletion and regeneration dynamics. We derive the modified Solow steady state in closed form and show that it depends on a thermo-ecological multiplier Ω = ϕ(τ) · ζ(H) · θ(H) that is strictly less than unity when thermodynamic waste and health damage are positive, where τ is waste intensity treated as a technology parameter. The steady-state capital intensity and output per worker are reduced by a factor that depends on pollution intensity, health capital, and the elasticity of damage. We characterize the resulting thermodynamic growth drag: a permanent downward shift of the balanced growth path, not a poverty trap, since the equilibrium is unique and stable. We define Thermo-GDP (a damage-adjusted output measure) and connect it to existing green accounting frameworks (SEEA, Adjusted Net Savings, Inclusive Wealth). Potential extensions to Ramsey optimal growth, Hotelling resource extraction, and DSGE environmental shocks are discussed.

title:
Effects of Natural Resources on Objective Well-being in Africa : The Moderating Role of Women’s
Representation in Parliament

detail.title:
Effects of Natural Resources on Objective Well-being in Africa : The Moderating Role of Women’s
Representation in Parliament
detail.abstract: Although the literature on the natural resource curse has extensively documented the effects of resource rents on economic growth and governance, the moderating role of women's political representation remains underexplored. To our knowledge, no study has examined the influence of women's parliamentary representation on the relationship between natural resources and objective well-being in Africa. This study investigates this issue using a panel of 30 African countries over the period 2000-2020. The analysis employs the Driscoll and Kraay (1998) estimator and Hansen's (1999) threshold model. The findings reveal that natural resources negatively and significantly affect objective wellbeing. However, this relationship is non-linear. The threshold model identifies a critical threshold of 25.70% women's representation in parliament: below this threshold, natural resources deteriorate objective well-being, whereas beyond it, their effect becomes positive and significant. These findings support the adoption of constitutional quotas guaranteeing 26% female representation in African parliaments.

title: Monetary Policy Responds to Economic News Text: Evidence from China
affiliations: , Zhejiang University and Zhejiang University

detail.title: Monetary Policy Responds to Economic News Text: Evidence from China
detail.abstract: This paper investigates whether and how economic news text serves as a viable supplement to central banks' information set. We employ topic modeling and machine learning to process over five million Chinese economic news articles and construct textual indicators. Our findings demonstrate that monetary policy responds significantly to textual indicators that provide incremental information beyond conventional numerical variables. Decomposition analysis reveals that policymakers exhibit greater sensitivity to newly arriving textual innovations than to historically accumulated narratives. When economic growth exceeds official targets, economic news text carries greater weight than numerical variables in policy formulation. The underlying mechanism driving these results is that news text captures information about market expectations and monetary policy perceptions, serving as a valuable input for policy formulation. We document that our arguments are not contingent on "central bank private information" or "central bank responses to public numerical information". Our resulting text-augmented policy shocks eliminate price puzzles in SVAR and underscore the critical role of news text in evaluating monetary policy effects on economic activity.

title: Yield Rates and Institutional Selectivity: Evidence from U.S. Universities

detail.title: Yield Rates and Institutional Selectivity: Evidence from U.S. Universities

detail.abstract: This paper examines the relationship between institutional characteristics and university acceptance rates using cross-sectional data from 1,039 U.S. universities obtained from the Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System (IPEDS). Multiple regression analysis is used to evaluate whether yield rate, retention rate, institutional size, and public university status are associated with institutional selectivity. The results indicate that yield rate exhibits a strong negative relationship with acceptance rate across all model specifications, suggesting that universities with stronger student demand tend to maintain lower acceptance rates. Retention rate also demonstrates a statistically significant negative relationship with selectivity, while larger institutions generally exhibit higher acceptance rates. An interaction term between yield rate and public university status suggests that the relationship between yield and selectivity differs between public and private institutions. Although the analysis is limited by its cross-sectional design, the findings provide evidence that measurable indicators of institutional demand and performance are strongly associated with college selectivity in the contemporary admissions environment.

The Mississippi River and Agricultural Trade:

detail.abstract: The Mississippi River system is a critical artery for U.S. agricultural commodities and intermediate inputs, connecting domestic production to Gulf export terminals. This paper quantifies the contribution of this navigation system to U.S. agricultural trade and welfare. We develop a multi-sector spatial general equilibrium model featuring inputoutput linkages, interstate labor mobility, and a bilateral trade cost technology that admits endogenous mode and transit hub substitution. We find that disabling commercial barge navigation on the Mississippi system reduces aggregate U.S. agricultural exports by 8.92 percent and production by 1.30 percent, driven by severe drops in cereal grain (-11.8 percent) and animal feed (-12.6 percent) exports. The aggregate U.S. welfare loss is 0.33 percent, or $29.2 billion annually, with spatial incidence heavily concentrated in Louisiana, West Virginia, and Corn Belt grain producers. Roughly one-third of the aggregate loss operates through input-output amplification via the fertilizer, coal and petroleum sectors. We estimate that the river's contribution to U.S. welfare exceeds total annualized federal cost of the system by a factor of eight, indicating an exceptionally high marginal productivity of federal capital.

title: The Commitment Trap: Institutional Reform in Fragmented Rentier States Evidence from Libya's Economic Governance Crisis
affiliations: Université de Poitiers

detail.title: The Commitment Trap: Institutional Reform in Fragmented Rentier States Evidence from Libya's Economic Governance Crisis
detail.abstract: Libya's rival elites have repeatedly coordinated on ceasefires and revenuesharing yet failed to build common economic institutions. This paper argues that in a fragmented rentier state, institutions like the budget and central bank are not merely administrative-they are assets of future political control. Strengthening them may raise welfare but also raises the value of capturing the state tomorrow. When elites cannot credibly commit to sharing a strengthened state, they prefer narrow bargains over current rents to deep bargains over institutional integration. The paper develops this argument in a dynamic framework, derives an endogenous mediation threshold above which deep cooperation becomes incentivecompatible, and shows that the threshold rises over time as elite capture deepens. Three episodes from Libya's post-2014 record-the rejection of the Mustafeed transparency mechanism (2022), the Central Bank leadership crisis (2024), and the sidelining of the Libyan Economic Expert Commission (2020-21)-provide structured case evidence. Elite resistance is selective (concentrated on institutions with high future-control value), categorical (framed as opposition to institutional architecture rather than to specific distributional losses), and tolerant of current costs (including oil shutdowns). These patterns suggest that future-capture concerns supplement, rather than replace, present-oriented motivations for institutional obstruction. The LEEC episode is particularly diagnostic: the same individuals who designed reform proposals from outside government abandoned them once they controlled the institutions from inside-a behavioral shift that the future-capture mechanism explains structurally.

title: Smart Contracts: Regulatory Challenges in the Russian Legal Framework and Their Overcoming through UNCITRAL Mechanisms
affiliations: MGIMO-University

detail.title: Smart Contracts: Regulatory Challenges in the Russian Legal Framework and Their Overcoming through UNCITRAL Mechanisms

keywords: Uncitral Model Law on Automated Contracting

detail.abstract:
The article examines the regulatory challenges associated with smart contracts in the Russian legal framework and explores the potential role of UNCITRAL instruments in addressing them. The main problem lies in the absence of a clear legal qualification of smart contracts in Russian law. Although smart contracts are used in practice and are indirectly reflected in certain provisions of the Civil Code, Russian legislation does not define them as automatically formed or automatically performed contracts. As a result, their regulation is largely shaped by the internal rules of digital platforms.
     The article argues that a smart contract should not be reduced either to a traditional contract, an electronic form of contract, or merely a method of performance. Rather, it should be treated as a sui generis legal and technological phenomenon. Particular attention is paid to the principles of technological neutrality, non-discrimination of automated transactions, attribution of actions performed by automated systems, and unexpected outcomes. The UNCITRAL Model Law on Automated Contracting may serve as an important reference point for developing a balanced Russian approach that combines statutory principles with platform-based regulation.

title: Loss Aversion, Elite Heterogeneity, and the Reversal of Democratic Transitions A Reference-dependent Theory of Regime Choice
affiliations: Université de Poitiers

detail.title: Loss Aversion, Elite Heterogeneity, and the Reversal of Democratic Transitions A Reference-dependent Theory of Regime Choice
detail.abstract: This paper develops a reference-dependent theory of democratic reversal. Democratic transitions impose short-run elite consumption losses before producing delayed institutional and growth dividends. When elites evaluate outcomes relative to a status-quo reference point, loss aversion creates a reversal threshold. I first derive this threshold for a representative elite, then introduce elite heterogeneity between reformers (who internalize citizen welfare) and opportunists (who do not). The model generates a type-contingent region in which political agency matters and a universal-reversal region in which loss aversion dominates both future gains and reformist motives. When types are private and citizen beliefs affect elite payoffs through a legitimacy channel, signaling shifts both type-specific thresholds upward by a common amount under symmetric belief feedback, preserving the typecontingent width and generating prior-dependent pooling outcomes characterized by explicit cutoffs from the Cho-Kreps Intuitive Criterion. The framework shows how transition costs, elite horizons, reformist motives, and citizen beliefs jointly determine democratic survival.

title: Retaliatory Taxation and the Birth of America's First Tax Treaty
affiliations: Peter A. Allard School of Law, the University of British Columbia

detail.title: Retaliatory Taxation and the Birth of America's First Tax Treaty

declarations.funderStatement: The research for this Article was supported by a Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada Insight Grant (No. 435-2022-0484).

detail.abstract: In 2025, the U.S. threatened retaliatory taxation against countries that adopt tax rules that "are extraterritorial or disproportionately affect American companies," both invoking a long-dormant provision of the Internal Revenue Code and proposing a new "revenge tax." This paper illuminates the origins of retaliatory taxation with new historical material that substantially expands our knowledge of the early history of U.S. international taxation. The investigation reveals a time when the type of legislation instantiated by the original retaliatory tax was the norm in the U.S., and when, by contrast, cooperation through tax treaties struggled to take root on American soil. This history underscores the deep fragility of the tax treaty as a mode of international cooperation for the U.S. because of the constitutional infirmities it suffers, the difficulty of separating the international provisions of the income tax from issues of international trade, and, most profoundly, the other policy options available to the U.S. as a hegemonic power. This paper concludes that just as the original retaliatory tax of 1934 was no isolated historical quirk, new retaliatory taxation may be no passing show of Trumpian histrionics.

title: Shareholder Rights and Constitutional Guarantees in Nigeria: A Critical Analysis of Minority Interest Protection Under the Companies and Allied Matters Act 2020
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Shareholder Rights and Constitutional Guarantees in Nigeria: A Critical Analysis of Minority Interest Protection Under the Companies and Allied Matters Act 2020
detail.abstract: This paper examines the constitutional and statutory protection available to minority shareholders under the companies and Allied Matters ACT 2020. The study analyses the traditional rule in FOSS V HARBOTTLE and its exceptions, while evaluating the remedies available to minority shareholders against oppression,unfair prejudice and abuse by majority shareholders such as fair hearing and property right as mechanisms for protecting minority interest. It identifies challenges including weak enforcement, judicial delay and corporate dominance and concludes that although CAMA 2020 has significantly improved minority shareholder protection, practical enforcement remains inadequate. The paper recommends stronger awareness and judicial reforms to enhance minority protection in Nigeria.

title: Oracle-anchored LVR Recapture with Selective Dutch Auction Repricing
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania

detail.title: Oracle-anchored LVR Recapture with Selective Dutch Auction Repricing
detail.abstract: Liquidity providers in automated market makers lose value when a pool price is stale relative to a faster reference market. This adverse-selection cost is known as loss-versus-rebalancing (LVR). We study a Uniswap v4 hook that uses an external oracle to detect stale pool states, charges stale-price trades with a square-root fee rule derived from one-step LVR accounting, and optionally routes repricing through a Dutch auction. The main comparison is against other v4hook designs on the same replay inputs: a base oracle-anchored hook without the auction path, a broad all-stale auction rule, and the proposed selective auction rule that opens only when the auction improves LP accounting relative to the base hook. On an observed-flow replay covering 54 multi-hour windows across seven Uniswap v3 pools (36 routine four-hour windows and 18 historical two-hour stress windows, roughly 180 hours of trading in total), the selective auction improves LP uplift versus the broad all-stale auction in 28 windows, leaves 26 unchanged, and worsens none. Its mean trigger rate is 0.9825%, compared with 5.8233% for the broad auction rule, while every triggered selective-auction window fills in the replay. A separate full-month October 2025 grid covering four pools, 89,220 swaps, and 8,784 oracle updates across 124 fourhour windows calibrates the auction layer and retains fixed-fee v3 only as a legacy leakage check.

title: ”Make it real”: How behavioral and financial costs shape environmental policy support
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Gothenburg - Centre for Collective Action (CeCAR), University of Gothenburg - Department of Political Science, University of Gothenburg, Wageningen University and Research (WUR), University of Economics Ho Chi Minh City, University of Gothenburg, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Bennett University

detail.title: ”Make it real”: How behavioral and financial costs shape environmental policy support
detail.abstract: Public concern about environmental degradation is widespread, yet translating this concern into support for effective policies remains a major challenge. This study examines how perceptions of personal costs and the framing of lifestyle changes influence policy acceptability in three countries of the Global South. We conducted an online survey experiment with around 5,000 respondents in Ghana, Vietnam, and Costa Rica. Participants were randomly assigned to one of several treatments highlighting behavioral, financial, or asset-related costs—or, alternatively, positive low-carbon options—across four lifestyle sectors: transport, food, fashion, and waste. Our results show that support for environmental policies declines significantly when personal costs are emphasized, especially financial ones. However, presenting realistic and appealing alternatives increases acceptability, suggesting that positive framing can offset cost aversion. These findings provide new evidence from under-studied regions on how policy design and communication can bridge the gap between environmental concern and actual support.

title: Is Inequality Inevitable? Trajectories of Development in Early Agricultural Societies
affiliations: Yeshiva University - Syms School of Business and University of Lille - CHU Lille

detail.title: Is Inequality Inevitable? Trajectories of Development in Early Agricultural Societies
detail.abstract: We propose a Malthusian model of conflict in the Neolithic to study the dynamics of inequality from the onset of agriculture. Societies evolve in a region where the total supply of land is fixed and undergo three distinct stages of development: An initial foraging stage, an expansion stage when arable land is abundant, and an encroachment stage when land becomes scarce, and societies compete for its control. For each stage, we characterize the division of economic surplus between elites and workers. Our main result is that inequality is not destined to rise with the adoption of agriculture: depending on the output elasticity of labor-our summary measure of workers' effective influence over the surplus-societies may follow trajectories that rise, fall, or exhibit a hump. Using data from 1,173 archaeological sites across six independent centers of agricultural origin, we document distinct regional paths consistent with the model. Inequality increased monotonically in West Asia and Europe, but followed inverse U-shaped patterns in South and Mesoamerica, as well as in East Asia. We argue that these heterogeneous trajectories reflect variation in a small set of ecological and technological parameters that shape workers' marginal productivity and, therefore, their bargaining power.

title: The Effect of LIHTC Developments on Surrounding Rents and Home Prices in Florida
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of Boston, Georgia Institute of Technology, Enterprise Community Partners, California State Polytechnic University, Pomona - Finance, Real Estate and Law Department, Occidental College, Econsult Solutions and SZ Consulting

detail.title: The Effect of LIHTC Developments on Surrounding Rents and Home Prices in Florida
detail.abstract: The prospect of new affordable rental housing in a neighborhood often triggers concerns among local homeowners, who fear the development's negative effect on home sale prices. Building upon an increasing body of research, we show that new rental developments financed with equity associated with the federal Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) have had a positive effect on surrounding home sale prices in metropolitan areas throughout Florida. Yet such positive effects raise the possibility that higher home sale prices may contribute to higher rents and thus make housing less affordable for market-rate renters. Using an extensive rental database, we examine the effects of the same LIHTC developments on rents in nearby market-rate multifamily properties. We find that, relative to prevailing market trends, the developments have helped decrease nearby market rents in some markets. Put differently, local market-rate rents in those areas were lower after the LIHTC development than the overall trends would suggest. While the LIHTC rent effects were not universal across markets, we do not find any statistically significant evidence that the developments increased nearby market-rate rents. The additional supply of rental units appears to have outweighed the potentially inflationary pressures resulting from an improved real estate market. These findings suggest that the rental and homeownership markets respond differently to the addition of new affordable units and that LIHTC housing simultaneously generates benefits for its tenants, nearby homeowners, and nearby marketrate renters.

title: Spatial distribution and influencing factors of vision impairment in children and adolescents in China, 2000–2019
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Spatial distribution and influencing factors of vision impairment in children and adolescents in China, 2000–2019
detail.abstract: Background and objective: Given that myopia has emerged as the leading cause of vision impairment among adolescents worldwide, yet remains underexplored in terms of systematic spatial analysis integrating natural and social environmental determinants. Therefore, this study aimed to determine the current prevalence of vision impairment among children and adolescents and to analyze its influencing factors.Methods: This study employed a repeated cross-sectional design using 150 province-year observations (30 provinces × 5 waves, 2000-2019) from the Chinese National Survey on Student Constitution and Health. We integrated the Health Ecological Model with a two-way fixed-effects Spatial Durbin Model (SDM) to analyze spatio-temporal patterns of vision impairment. Additional analyses included global and local Moran’s I statistics for spatial autocorrelation assessment and multiple spatial weight matrices for robustness testing, all conducted using STATA 15.0.Results: From 2000 to 2019, the detection rate of vision impairment among China’s children and adolescents exhibited a continuous upward trend, with a marked deceleration observed after 2014. Moran’s I statistics revealed significant positive spatial autocorrelation and provincial clustering patterns. The SDM results indicated that spatial indirect effects substantially dominated local direct effects. Furthermore, per capita GDP, PM2.5 concentrations, and urban population density demonstrated robust associations with neighboring regions’ vision impairment rates across multiple spatial weight specifications.Conclusion: These spatial patterns may suggest the need to consider regional-scale approaches to vision impairment prevention, including cross-provincial medical resource coordination, investment in outdoor infrastructure in high-density urban areas, and coordinated regional air quality management.

title:
The Independent Security Study under Treasury Regulation §1.132-5(m) 
A Practitioner Framework for Audit-defensible Executive Protection Tax Compliance in the Post-Thompson Era

detail.title:
The Independent Security Study under Treasury Regulation §1.132-5(m) 
A Practitioner Framework for Audit-defensible Executive Protection Tax Compliance in the Post-Thompson Era

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Avren, Inc. is an independent security study practice. It performs Independent Security Studies under Treasury Regulation §1.132-5(m) for clients seeking to satisfy the procedural prerequisites discussed in this paper. As such, the author institution has a direct commercial interest in the subject matter. The framework set out in this paper is intended as a structured restatement of existing law and regulation; it is not legal or tax advice, and no advisor-client relationship is created by this paper.

detail.abstract: The December 2024 killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, followed by the subsequent shooting incidents at corporate offices in 2025, has produced the largest single-year repricing of executive security risk in modern American corporate history. Median disclosed executive security spending among S&P 500 companies more than doubled between 2021 and 2024, the number of companies disclosing security perquisites rose by 27.8 percent year over year, and at least fourteen large-cap issuers initiated new security programs in 2025. Beneath this operational surge sits a narrow and underexamined body of tax law: Treasury Regulation §1.132-5(m), which conditions the gross-income exclusion of employer-provided security on a sequence of procedural prerequisites that culminate in an "Independent Security Study." Where the requirements are satisfied, an "overall security program" is deemed to exist, the executive may exclude the value of qualified protection from income as a working condition fringe, and personal use of employer-provided aircraft is valued under §1.61-21(g) at a capped 200 percent aircraft multiple rather than full charter or non-capped SIFL rates. The procedural prerequisites are exacting: an objectively qualified independent consultant, an objective analysis of facts and circumstances, a written report recommending 24-hour protection, and reasonable implementation by the employer. Yet the published guidance on what these requirements actually entail is sparse, and the existing literature on §1.132-5(m) consists almost entirely of summary explanations rather than operational frameworks. This paper supplies that framework. It restates the statutory and regulatory architecture, articulates the substantive content of each procedural element, identifies the audit-defensibility considerations that examiners and corporate tax departments now confront, and addresses the disclosure interplay with Item 402 of Regulation S-K. It closes with a reassessment cadence calibrated to the post-Thompson threat environment and a documentation framework intended to be used by practicing tax advisors, security consultants, corporate secretaries, and audit teams.

reference: NLUD Journal of Legal Studies Vol. 3, 2021, Pp. 111
title: Reflections on Information Influence Operations and Illegal Intervention

detail.title: Reflections on Information Influence Operations and Illegal Intervention

publicationDetails.detailsText: NLUD Journal of Legal Studies Vol. 3, 2021, Pp. 111

detail.abstract: The dust is yet to settle on the issue of the applicability of the United Nations Charter to cyberspace, but international law is already facing its most vexing issue yet in cyberspace -foreign information influence operations. Thrust into focus by the Russian interference into the US elections in 2016, this issue has sparked a furious debate in the international community, with several legal scholars recommending the prohibition on intervention in the internal affairs of States as a tool to regulate this new phenomenon. However, the intervention prohibition is not so easily applied to foreign information influence operations. This article identifies three hurdles to this argument - the coercion criterion, a lack of clarity in States 'views and difficulties in attribution. The article also highlights the flaws in current scholarly approaches to the issue and proposes a modified, more suitable version of the deception test for acceptance by States.

reference: ADB Economics Working Paper Series No. 851
title: The Great Reallocation Revisited: How Foreign Direct Investment Is (and Is Not) Shifting amid Heightened Geopolitical Tensions
affiliations: Asian Development Bank, Dartmouth College - Tuck School of Business, Williams College, United Nations - Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) and UNCTAD

detail.title: The Great Reallocation Revisited: How Foreign Direct Investment Is (and Is Not) Shifting amid Heightened Geopolitical Tensions

publicationDetails.detailsText: ADB Economics Working Paper Series No. 851

detail.abstract: This paper examines how global greenfield foreign direct investment (FDI) flows are evolving amid rising geoeconomic fragmentation. We use difference-in-differences and event study approaches to analyze changes in FDI around key bilateral inflection points. We find a decline in FDI from the US and broader Group of Seven Plus (G7+) into the PRC, concentrated in trade-exposed, efficiency-seeking sectors. Investment diversion—particularly from the PRC to Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) members and Latin America—is evident, but this growth was concentrated in less global value chain (GVC)-integrated activities, suggesting that GVC links may act as a constraint on investment relocation. These findings suggest that while tensions may be reshaping global investment, GVC dependencies are likely limiting firms’ ability to reallocate production at scale, making the “great reallocation” least evident where it was most expected.

title: Engineering Habit at Scale: The Hook Model, Cognitive Ergonomics, and the Ethical Boundaries of behavioral Product Design
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Engineering Habit at Scale: The Hook Model, Cognitive Ergonomics, and the Ethical Boundaries of behavioral Product Design
detail.abstract: Behavioral design techniques are now standard practice in digital product development. Eyal's (2014) Hook Model, which engineers habitual engagement through trigger-action-rewardinvestment loops, has been adopted across consumer and enterprise applications. Yet a troubling pattern recurs: the same behavioral techniques that create genuine user value in one context produce extractive, manipulative outcomes in another. A fitness app that builds healthy exercise habits uses the same Hook architecture as a social media platform engineered to maximize timeon-site regardless of user wellbeing. Ethics scholarship has treated this as a binary question (ethical or not), while the product management literature has treated behavioral design as universally beneficial once properly implemented. Neither accounts for a specific, consequential factor: the lifecycle phase of the product and the structural alignment between business incentives and user welfare. This paper addresses that gap by integrating the Hook Model with Norman's (2013) cognitive ergonomics framework and proposing the Manipulation Matrix as a formal ethical boundary condition. I argue that the ethical permissibility of behavioral engineering is lifecycle-phase-dependent: it is appropriate only after product-market fit is established, and contraindicated before that point, where it would engineer habit around unvalidated value. Three propositions are developed linking phase-dependent ethical boundaries to user satisfaction outcomes across technology-intensive product organizations. Implications for product management practice, regulatory policy, and AI system design are discussed.

title: Membership Turnover and Operational Reliability in Multi-partner Systems: Evidence from Venture Capital Syndicates
affiliations: , Purdue University - Krannert School of Management and University of Toronto

detail.title: Membership Turnover and Operational Reliability in Multi-partner Systems: Evidence from Venture Capital Syndicates
detail.abstract: Entrepreneurial ventures rely on a distributed finance supply chain in which multiple investors coordinate capital provision, monitoring, and strategic guidance. The reliability of this system depends on stable coordination and information-processing processes among upstream investors who collectively support downstream ventures. When investors enter or exit these multi-partner systems, established coordination and communication processes may be disrupted, increasing process instability and reducing operational reliability. Using a panel of 9,281 U.S. ventures and 237,432 venture-quarter observations from 1980-2023, we find that a one-standard-deviation increase in syndicate turnover reduces a venture's likelihood of securing follow-on financing by 65%. We show that network architecture shapes system resilience: greater network constraint buffers the disruptive effects of turnover by stabilizing coordination and communication processes and preserving reliable information exchange, whereas stronger network faultlines amplify these effects by fragmenting communication pathways and weakening information integration across investors. Further, we show that these coordination disruptions significantly lengthen financing cycle time and subsequently reduce the likelihood of successful venture exit through IPO or acquisition. By conceptualizing VC syndicates as multi-partner operational systems, this study extends operations management research on disruption propagation, coordination reliability, and network resilience in distributed systems.

reference: European Corporate Governance Institute - Law Working Paper No. 942/2026
title: The EU Inc.: A Half-Naked 28th Regime
affiliations: ,  and Leibniz Institute for Financial Research SAFE

detail.title: The EU Inc.: A Half-Naked 28th Regime

publicationDetails.detailsText: European Corporate Governance Institute - Law Working Paper No. 942/2026
publicationDetails.journalName: European Corporate Governance Institute (ECGI) - Law Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
The European Commission’s proposal for a 28th corporate law regime (“EU Inc.”) has been presented as a cornerstone of the Union’s strategy to foster innovation, retain high-growth firms, and strengthen Europe’s venture capital ecosystem. 

This article argues that the proposal falls substantially short of those ambitions. Building on prior work showing how rigid corporate law rules can impede venture capital contracting and startup financing, the article evaluates whether EU Inc. delivers the self-contained, innovation-oriented legal framework envisioned by the Letta and Draghi Reports. It contends that the proposal has drifted from a targeted instrument for startups and scale-ups toward a broadly available corporate form designed to accommodate the interests of established firms and national constituencies. 

While the proposal introduces several welcome innovations—including non-par value shares, compatibility with SAFE-style financing instruments, harmonised employee equity arrangements, and reduced reliance on notarisation in key transactions—it simultaneously preserves extensive references to national law, broad Member State discretion, and procedural compromises that undermine legal uniformity and cross-border certainty. The article further argues that the proposal’s emphasis on digitalisation over substantive legal integration, its broad scope, and its fragmented adjudicatory and governance architecture risk reproducing many of the shortcomings that frustrated earlier attempts to create pan-European corporate forms. Rather than constituting the transformative framework required to support Europe’s innovation economy, EU Inc. emerges as a modest and incomplete reform. 

The article concludes that, unless substantially strengthened during the legislative process, the proposal is unlikely to alter the incentives that continue to drive innovative European firms toward foreign jurisdictions and legal frameworks.

title: Enterprise Financial Crime Detection Through Explainable AI: A Case Study of Consolidation and Automation in Multi-Institutional Environments

detail.title: Enterprise Financial Crime Detection Through Explainable AI: A Case Study of Consolidation and Automation in Multi-Institutional Environments

detail.abstract: This article examines the architecture, implementation, and regulatory outcomes of enterprisescale financial crime detection systems through the lens of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). Drawing on a decade of practitioner experience consolidating fragmented transaction monitoring infrastructures across multiple business units and regulatory jurisdictions, this case study demonstrates how explainable hybrid ensemble frameworks reduce false-positive rates by 60% while improving detection accuracy to 98.5% across high-risk typologies. The paper addresses a critical gap in financial crime literature: the relationship between model interpretability, regulatory compliance, and operational efficiency in multi-institutional environments. Unlike prior research emphasizing pure predictive performance, this work demonstrates that governance-aligned explainability is essential for institutional legitimacy, regulator confidence, and sustainable crime prevention. Through detailed analysis of system consolidation, control propagation, and alert generation workflows, the article contributes both methodological insights for practitionerresearchers and policy recommendations for regulators overseeing AI-driven financial crime systems.

title: Optimal Multiple-stopping Strategies for Dynamic Bond Ladder Portfolios
affiliations: , University of California Santa Barbara, University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB) and University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB)

detail.title: Optimal Multiple-stopping Strategies for Dynamic Bond Ladder Portfolios
detail.abstract:
Bond ladder strategies are widely used in fixed income portfolio construction, particularly in insurance asset-liability management and pension investing. Traditional ladder implementations rely on deterministic rebalancing rules and cannot adapt dynamically to evolving yield curve conditions. 

This paper develops an adaptive bond ladder framework in which portfolio interventions such as selling, stripping, and purchasing bonds are formulated as a multiple optimal stopping problem. The resulting stochastic control problem is driven by yield curve dynamics estimated from historical data via a dynamic Nelson-Siegel representation.

To evaluate stopping decisions, we derive analytical approximations to the distribution of portfolio gains using Gram-Charlier density expansions. These approximations allow the expected stopping value to be computed in closed form from moments of the gain distribution. Dominance-probability selection rules are introduced to determine the optimal bond and action at each intervention time. 

Monte Carlo simulations are used to estimate the required moments and to benchmark the analytical approximations. The results demonstrate that the proposed approach delivers accurate value function estimates while achieving substantial computational efficiency relative to brute-force simulation. 

The framework provides a tractable method for integrating dynamic decision rules into bond ladder management and is particularly relevant for insurers and institutional investors operating in multicurve fixed income environments.

title: Fundamental Limitations of Fixed-Budget Best-Arm Identification

detail.title: Fundamental Limitations of Fixed-Budget Best-Arm Identification
detail.abstract: In fixed-budget best-arm identification, also known as ranking and selection, an algorithm has a sampling budget to distribute across K arms. Each sample provides noisy feedback about that arm's mean, and the goal is to identify the arm with the largest mean. A common performance benchmark is the static oracle: a non-adaptive strategy that knows the means in advance and chooses fixed sampling proportions to maximize the exponential decay rate of the probability of incorrect identification. Several adaptive algorithms have been constructed such that their sampling proportions converge to the static oracle proportions. However, it has remained open whether any algorithm could match the static oracle's error decay rate uniformly across all problem instances. We answer this in the negative. For any K ≥ 3 and for rewards drawn from any one-parameter natural exponential family, we show that for any algorithm, there is at least one instance where the error decay rate is at most 1/(1 + log(K)/8) times that of the static oracle. This also answers the open question posed by Qin (2022), showing that fixed-budget best-arm identification does not admit a complexity.

title: Academic Citation Infrastructure: Infrastructure-Level Interventions for Generative Engine Optimization
affiliations: ILLIXIS (illixis.io)

detail.title: Academic Citation Infrastructure: Infrastructure-Level Interventions for Generative Engine Optimization
detail.abstract: Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) research has focused exclusively on content-level interventions: adding statistics, citing sources, using authoritative tone, and structuring text for extraction. No peer-reviewed GEO work has proposed infrastructure-level interventions for increasing AI system citation rates. Scattered practitioner recommendations for individual tactics (DOI deposits, ScholarlyArticle schema, repository placement) have emerged independently but remain unconnected, unanalyzed, and untested. This paper proposes the first formal framework for what we term Academic Citation Infrastructure (ACI): the deliberate attachment of scholarly publishing infrastructure to commercial content. ACI unifies four techniques into a coherent strategy: methods-paper formatting,   BibTeX/RIS citation file generation, Zenodo DOI mirroring, and ScholarlyArticle schema markup. Quantitative evidence from source framing studies, repository discoverability research, and LLM search selection analysis supports the underlying mechanisms. This paper unifies these scattered tactics into a testable framework and, as a recursive demonstration, implements all four techniques on itself.

title: A Systematic Review of Trustworthy AI for Marketing Measurement in Attribution Media Mix Modeling and Privacy Preserving Methods
affiliations: University of Rochester, Stanford University and

detail.title: A Systematic Review of Trustworthy AI for Marketing Measurement in Attribution Media Mix Modeling and Privacy Preserving Methods
detail.abstract: Marketing measurement faces a triple disruption: privacy regulations restrict user-level data, artificial intelligence transforms modeling capabilities, and largescale field experiments expose systematic biases in platform-reported advertising effectiveness. This systematic review synthesizes 108 studies (2010-2026) on how AI and machine learning reshape measurement across multi-touch attribution, media mix modeling, causal calibration, and privacy-preserving measurement. We develop a two-dimensional taxonomy mapping AI techniques to measurement functions and propose a "Measure-Validate-Protect" (MVP) framework that adapts NIST AI trustworthiness dimensions to marketing contexts. Three findings emerge. First, deep learning attribution improves predictive accuracy but remains causally unidentified without experimental calibration. Second, neural media mix models can outperform traditional Bayesian frameworks in selected benchmark and production settings, yet causal credibility depends on external validation and generalization remains under-tested. Third, privacy-preserving techniques impose measurable accuracy costs: differential privacy reduces precision by 2-33% depending on privacy budget, while federated approaches have retained roughly 90-95% of centralized performance in documented deployments. We identify gaps at the intersection of causal validity and privacy compliance and propose a research agenda for trustworthy marketing AI.

title: Rational Avoidance, Irrational Engagement: On the Economic Rationality of Social Media Use

detail.title: Rational Avoidance, Irrational Engagement: On the Economic Rationality of Social Media Use

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has no personal or financial relationship with other people or organizations that may have or could be perceived to have influenced their study.
declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by the DMSB behavioral lab and grant program.

detail.abstract: This paper tests the economic rationality of social media use as per the Generalized Axiom of Revealed Preference (GARP). Economic rationality is one prerequisite for the effectiveness of taxation and price-based policies to regulate consumption. In a series of four incentive-compatible online and laboratory experiments, including one with a Gen-Z sample, I find that, on average, time allocation decisions between social media use and working for extrinsic rewards appear largely consistent with GARP , and more so than comparable financial decisions under risk of the same individual. This apparent rationality, however, is primarily driven by many consumers who opt out of social media use altogether. Conversely, engaging with social media causes consumers to exhibit significantly lower economic rationality, particularly at higher levels of use. Together with overall inelastic demand, these results suggest that social media consumption may respond only weakly to changes in costs and incentives: some consumers exhibit low price elasticity, while others display limited consistency with revealed-preference rationality. Behavioral interventions, by contrast, appear to shift usage behavior effectively, as I show experimentally. I discuss the results against the background of current discussions about social media bans.

title: Data Challenges in Institutional Rankings: Evidence from HEIS in the Marathwada Region

detail.title: Data Challenges in Institutional Rankings: Evidence from HEIS in the Marathwada Region

detail.abstract:
This study examines the data-related challenges faced by Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) in institutional ranking frameworks, with special emphasis on the Marathwada region of Maharashtra. The study focuses on three key issues: limited understanding of ranking parameters among faculty, inadequate technical infrastructure for data management, and a compliance-oriented approach arising from compulsory participation in frameworks such as the National Institutional Ranking Framework (NIRF). The research adopts a qualitative, observation-based approach, drawing on the researcher’s direct involvement in institutional data processes from 2016 to 2025. 

The findings reveal that faculty members often perceive data collection as an administrative obligation rather than a quality enhancement activity, resulting in superficial compilation and inconsistencies in data submission. Additionally, many institutions—particularly in rural areas—lack essential digital infrastructure, including Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) systems and centralized data management tools, leading to inefficiencies and reliability concerns. The study further highlights that mandatory participation has shifted institutional focus toward procedural compliance rather than meaningful quality improvement.

 To address these challenges, the study recommends strengthening Institutional Quality Assurance Cells (IQACs), implementing structured faculty development programs, promoting digital infrastructure, and enhancing awareness regarding the purpose and utility of ranking frameworks. The study underscores the importance of integrating data-driven decision-making and continuous monitoring to improve institutional performance and educational outcomes.

title: A Probabilistic Feasibility Assessment of Semiconductor Fabrication Plant Expansion Using Monte Carlo-Integrated DCF Analysis
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: A Probabilistic Feasibility Assessment of Semiconductor Fabrication Plant Expansion Using Monte Carlo-Integrated DCF Analysis
detail.abstract: Investors face risks in greenfield semiconductor fabrication plant expansion such as construction delays, yield ramp uncertainty and sudden escalation of operating costs. Deterministic cash flow models (DCF) fail to take these uncertainties into account and hence understate downside exposure. To address this, Monte Carlo based DCF model has been constructed in which we took construction delay as a continuous PERT(0,3,18) distribution. Operating costs were set to evolve as a Geometric Brownian motion (GBM) process and subjected it to Ito volatility drag, and also captured joint cost-yield dependence using a Clayton copula configured to Kendall's τ ≈ 0.45. Then, three geographic volatility regimes were chosen (σ ∈ {0.15, 0.28, 0.40}) for proxy supply chain conditions across the United States/Europe, India/South East Asia, and Taiwan/South Korea. After running 10,000 simulations, the baseline (United States/Europe) returned a mean NPV of USD -394.73 million, a median of USD -393.63 million, a fifth percentile of USD -853.30 million, and a P95 of USD +60.34 million; concluded that only 8.1% of runs are NPV positive. An essential takeaway of this paper was that the GBM cost of escalation against fixed wafer price revenue generated a perennially left-skewed NPV (Net Present Value) distribution which is a tail-risk structure that deterministic DCF suppressed when it substituted the mean cost path for the entire stochastic distribution. This resulted in a probabilistic feasibility map that lets capital allocators compare tail exposure across various geographic scenarios under any revised set of assumptions.

title: Does the Veblen Effect Exist? An Analysis of its Likelihood in Luxury Consumption and Potential Consequences for Pricing Management
affiliations: The Bridge to Luxury

detail.title: Does the Veblen Effect Exist? An Analysis of its Likelihood in Luxury Consumption and Potential Consequences for Pricing Management
detail.abstract: Luxury pricing follows management rules that are different from fast-moving consumer goods. In particular, the Veblen effect – hypothesising that higher prices prompt higher consumer demand – has fascinated academia and business practice for decades within the context of theories such as conspicuous consumption or social signalling. This article presents a new assessment demonstrating that this effect – if it exists at all – is only temporary and limited in scope as exemplified by the empirical data of the Swiss watch industry and sports car manufacturer Ferrari from 2000 to 2025. To this end, the analysis first defines the concept of luxury within the framework of an innovative semantic system. It describes the specific characteristics of luxury pricing, focusing particularly on consumer needs and their potential relevance for the assumed existence of the Veblen effect. As the analysis concludes that the effect barely exists, implying a much more complex context for luxury pricing, the article outlines specifics in luxury pricing management.
